q: Fabrikam's security policy forbids storing passwords, or hashes of passwords, in the cloud, and the team will not build federation infrastructure. Sign-in to Entra ID applications must keep working if any single on-premises server fails. Which design meets these requirements?
opts: Pass-through authentication, with agents installed on multiple domain-joined hosts
AD FS federation, with two federation servers behind a load balancer
Password hash synchronization, with a second Entra Connect server in staging mode
Pass-through authentication, with one agent on the Microsoft Entra Connect server
why: Pass-through authentication validates each password against on-premises AD, so no password or hash is stored in the cloud and no federation farm is needed. Because sign-in fails when no agent is reachable, installing agents on more than one host removes the single point of failure. A single agent meets the password rule but fails the "any single server" requirement. Password hash synchronization stores a hash of the on-premises password hash in Entra ID, which the policy forbids, and a staging-mode server does not change that. AD FS keeps passwords on premises but is exactly the federation infrastructure the team refuses to build.

q: Contoso's 25 administrators permanently hold Global Administrator or subscription Owner. Auditors want privileged access to be time-limited, justified, and approved, with MFA required at the moment of use. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
opts: Replace the roles with narrower custom roles at management group scope
Convert the permanent assignments to eligible assignments in PIM
Enable a sign-in risk policy for administrator accounts
Require approval, justification, and MFA in the PIM role settings
Run a monthly access review of the permanent assignments
why: Eligible assignments remove standing access, and the PIM role settings enforce approval, justification, and MFA at activation with a bounded duration; together they meet every audit requirement. A monthly access review only recertifies standing assignments, so the access stays standing between reviews. Narrower custom roles change what is permitted, not when or for how long. A sign-in risk policy reacts to suspicious sign-ins and neither time-limits nor approves privileged elevation.

q: A policy assigned at a management group must make sure every storage account has a diagnostic setting that sends logs to a central workspace. Teams create accounts constantly, creation must never be blocked, and a diagnostic setting is a separate resource from the storage account. Which effect should the policy use?
opts: DeployIfNotExists
Modify
Append
AuditIfNotExists
why: DeployIfNotExists looks for a related resource, here the diagnostic setting, and deploys it when it is missing, without blocking creation of the storage account. AuditIfNotExists performs the same related-resource check but only reports noncompliance; nothing gets deployed. Modify and Append change properties or tags on the resource being evaluated and cannot create a separate resource. Accounts that were already noncompliant before the assignment are corrected by running a remediation task.

q: A conglomerate has three subsidiaries, each with several subscriptions and its own IT team managing its own policies and RBAC. The parent company must enforce one mandatory tagging policy on every subscription, assigned once, and subsidiary teams must not be able to remove it. Which structure should you recommend?
opts: A separate Entra tenant per subsidiary, with the tagging policy assigned in each tenant
A parent management group with a child group per subsidiary, assigning the tagging policy at the parent
All subscriptions directly under the tenant root group, with the tagging policy assigned to each subscription
A management group per subsidiary, with the tagging policy assigned separately to each one
why: A policy assigned at the parent management group is created once, inherited by every child group and subscription, and cannot be removed by subsidiary administrators who have no rights at the parent scope, while each child group still holds that subsidiary's own policies and RBAC. Assigning the policy separately per child group repeats the work and leaves each subsidiary's owners able to delete their own copy. Subscriptions directly under the root also need one assignment each and give no subsidiary-level grouping. Separate tenants multiply identity administration, and a policy assignment cannot span tenants.

q: A healthcare group monitors everything through one Log Analytics workspace in East US. Its German clinical subsidiary must keep log data inside Germany, control its own access and retention, and still run its own KQL queries and alerts. How should you change the design?
opts: Send the subsidiary's logs to a storage account in Germany through a diagnostic setting
Keep the single workspace and restrict the subsidiary's tables with table-level access control
Keep the single workspace and set a longer retention period on the subsidiary's tables
Create a workspace in Germany West Central for the subsidiary and keep the central one for the rest
why: A workspace is bound to one region, so only a dedicated workspace in a German region keeps the data in Germany; it carries its own access and retention settings, and the subsidiary can query and alert on it directly. Table-level access control in the shared workspace still stores the data in East US. A longer table retention changes how long data stays, not where it lives. Archiving to a German storage account satisfies residency but gives up the interactive queries and alerts the subsidiary needs.

q: Contractors from partner firms request access themselves to three applications and a SharePoint site for the length of their contract. A manager must approve each request, and the access must be removed on the contract end date without anyone revoking it by hand. Which Entra ID Governance feature fits?
opts: A dynamic group whose membership rule checks a contractor attribute
A recurring access review with results applied automatically
An entitlement management access package with an expiration date
PIM eligible assignments with a fixed end date
why: An access package bundles the applications and site, supports a request-and-approval workflow, and its assignments expire on their own. A recurring access review can remove access when its results are applied automatically, but it only runs on a schedule and offers no request, approval, or bundling. A dynamic group grants access while an attribute matches, with no approval step and no end date tied to the contract. PIM eligible assignments govern privileged roles, not application and site access for external users.

q: Operations needs an alert within a minute when a VM's CPU stays above 90%. Security needs to join sign-in events, firewall logs, and VM events across six months of data. Which pairing of Azure Monitor capabilities fits?
opts: An activity log alert for CPU; the Activity log for the joins
A metric alert rule on the CPU metric; KQL queries over a Log Analytics workspace
A metric alert for CPU; Metrics Explorer with dimension splitting for the joins
A log search alert on the Perf table for CPU; Metrics Explorer for the joins
why: Platform metrics are lightweight numeric time series evaluated every minute, so a metric alert is the fast, cheap way to catch a CPU threshold, while joining several record types across months is exactly what Log Analytics and KQL do. A log search alert can watch CPU but adds ingestion and query latency, and Metrics Explorer cannot join record types. The Activity log records control-plane operations, not performance or security events. Splitting a metric by dimension is not a join, and platform metrics are kept for a limited period.

q: Contoso is building its first enterprise Azure environment. Every new application subscription must start with the same management group placement, policies, RBAC, and a connection to a shared hub network, with no setup work by the application teams. Which approach should you recommend?
opts: One shared subscription with a resource group per team and Azure Policy assigned to each group
A Bicep template that each application team runs to deploy a spoke VNet peered to the hub network
An Azure landing zone, with a platform connectivity subscription and new subscriptions created under governed management groups
A management group hierarchy with a policy initiative and RBAC roles assigned at the top level
why: A landing zone packages all the pieces: a management group hierarchy carrying inherited policy and RBAC, platform subscriptions hosting the hub network and identity, and a repeatable way to place each new subscription into that structure so it starts governed and connected. A management group hierarchy with policy and RBAC covers governance but delivers no hub connectivity. A template that application teams run themselves covers networking only, depends on each team running it, and brings no governance inheritance. A shared subscription with per-team resource groups blurs billing and scale boundaries and has no new subscriptions to inherit anything.

q: A tenant uses pass-through authentication and also turns on password hash synchronization. If every pass-through authentication agent goes offline, Entra ID does not automatically start validating sign-ins with the synchronized hashes.
opts: True
False
why: Password hash synchronization enabled alongside pass-through authentication is not an automatic fallback; an administrator would have to switch the sign-in method. Resilience therefore comes from running several authentication agents, since a single agent is a single point of failure, not from having hash sync switched on. A tenant that needs sign-in to survive an on-premises outage with no intervention chooses password hash synchronization as its sign-in method.

q: A Conditional Access policy can be applied when an administrator activates a PIM-eligible role, so activation can demand a stricter control, such as a compliant device, than an ordinary sign-in does.
opts: True
False
why: PIM role settings can require a Conditional Access authentication context at activation, so a policy bound to that context, for example one requiring a compliant device, is evaluated when the role is activated. PIM controls when privilege is granted and Conditional Access controls the conditions of access, so they are layered rather than substitutes for each other.

q: A user holds Contributor at subscription scope. Assigning that user the Reader role on one resource group makes the user read-only in that resource group.
opts: True
False
why: Azure RBAC is additive: role assignments combine, and a narrower-scope assignment never removes permissions inherited from a broader scope, so the user stays a Contributor in that resource group. To make the group read-only for that user, narrow the broad assignment instead, for example by assigning Contributor only on the resource groups where it is needed.

q: Which two statements about Privileged Identity Management (PIM) are true? (Choose two.)
opts: The scope of an activation is chosen by the user at activation time, regardless of the scope of the eligibility
An activated eligible assignment ends automatically when the configured activation duration elapses
It manages eligible assignments for Azure resource roles, such as Owner on a subscription, as well as Entra directory roles
Approval workflows are available for Entra directory roles but not for Azure resource roles
A user must pass an access review before each activation of an eligible role
why: PIM covers both directory roles and Azure resource roles, and every activation is time-bound: it expires when the configured duration ends. Approval can be required for both kinds of role. Access reviews are a separate periodic recertification and do not gate each activation, and an activation cannot exceed the scope at which the user was made eligible.

q: Which two statements about Azure Policy effects are true? (Choose two.)
opts: A remediation task is how resources found noncompliant by a DeployIfNotExists or Modify policy are corrected after the fact
Policy effects are evaluated only when a resource is created, so existing resources are never assessed
After a Deny policy is assigned, resources that already violate it stay in place and show as noncompliant
A Deny policy assigned at a management group deletes noncompliant resources already deployed in its subscriptions
The Audit effect blocks noncompliant creation requests but still allows updates to existing resources
why: Deny acts on create and update requests; resources that already exist are assessed by compliance scans, stay in place, and are reported as noncompliant. Resources flagged by DeployIfNotExists or Modify policies are fixed by running a remediation task. Deny never deletes anything, Audit never blocks a request, and compliance scans do evaluate existing resources.

q: Which two statements about Azure management groups are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Each management group is its own billing boundary and receives a separate invoice
A subscription can have only one parent management group at a time
A management group hierarchy can span more than one Entra tenant
A policy assignment or role assignment at a management group is inherited by the subscriptions beneath it
A subscription can sit under several management groups so that it inherits policy from each of them
why: A subscription has exactly one parent at a time, which keeps inheritance unambiguous, and policy and RBAC assignments flow downward from a management group to everything beneath it. A subscription cannot have several parents, a hierarchy lives inside a single tenant, and management groups are a governance scope rather than a billing boundary; invoicing follows billing accounts and profiles.

q: A company has 15 policy definitions covering tagging, allowed resource types, and encryption, using a mix of Deny, Audit, and DeployIfNotExists effects. All 15 must be assigned together to every new subscription and reported on as a single compliance score. What should you use?
opts: A policy initiative (policy set definition) containing the 15 definitions, assigned at a management group
One custom definition whose rule combines the conditions of all 15 policies
The 15 definitions assigned separately at a management group so new subscriptions inherit them
A Bicep template that creates the 15 policy assignments on each new subscription
why: An initiative bundles the definitions into one assignable unit with shared parameters and rolls compliance up into one view; assigning it at a management group makes new subscriptions inherit it. Separate assignments at the management group would also be inherited, but they remain 15 assignments to manage and report on. A single custom definition cannot merge rules that use different effects and would lose per-policy compliance detail. A template that creates assignments per subscription still produces 15 assignments each time.

q: Contoso federates most users through AD FS and requires MFA through Conditional Access for every administrator. Leadership wants a guaranteed way to regain admin control if a Conditional Access misconfiguration, an MFA outage, or an on-premises failure blocks every normal sign-in. What should you create?
opts: Cloud-only Global Administrator accounts excluded from Conditional Access, with strong unique credentials and sign-in alerts
Global Administrator accounts synchronized from on-premises AD, excluded from Conditional Access and closely monitored
An eligible Global Administrator role in PIM for the CIO, activated with MFA when an emergency arises
Guest accounts from the managed service provider's tenant, assigned Global Administrator for emergencies
why: Break-glass accounts must not depend on anything that can fail together with normal sign-in: they are cloud-only, so an AD FS or sync failure cannot affect them, excluded from Conditional Access, protected by strong credentials, and monitored so any use triggers an alert. Synchronized accounts still depend on on-premises infrastructure. A PIM-eligible role needs MFA to activate, which may be the very thing that is broken, and leaves no account that can always sign in. Guests from another tenant depend on that tenant and remain subject to Conditional Access.

q: A diagnostic setting can send a regional resource's logs to a Log Analytics workspace in a different region, but a storage account destination must be in the same region as the resource.
opts: True
False
why: Workspace destinations are not tied to the monitored resource's region, which is why one central workspace can collect from many regions; storage account and event hub destinations must be co-located with the resource. A single diagnostic setting can also send to several destinations at once.

q: Contoso wants MFA required only when employees sign in to Microsoft 365 from unmanaged devices outside the corporate network, with legacy authentication blocked for everyone. Which should you configure?
opts: Security defaults, with legacy authentication blocked tenant-wide
Per-user MFA set to Enforced for every employee
Conditional Access policies with device and location conditions
A named location that lists the trusted corporate IP ranges
why: Conditional Access evaluates signals such as device state and location at sign-in and then applies a control, so it can require MFA only in the risky case and block legacy authentication through a separate policy. Security defaults apply one fixed baseline to everyone and cannot be limited to unmanaged devices outside the network. Per-user MFA is all-or-nothing and cannot consider device or location. A named location is only an input that a Conditional Access policy can use; on its own it enforces nothing.

q: A company uses PIM for just-in-time elevation. Each quarter, the role owner must document a decision on whether each eligible administrator still needs the role, and those who do not should lose eligibility. What should you add?
opts: A Conditional Access policy requiring a compliant device when the role is activated
A quarterly access review of the role's eligible assignments, with decisions applied automatically
A PIM role setting that makes every eligible assignment expire after 90 days
An entitlement management access package for the role, with a 90-day expiration
why: An access review has the role owner or another reviewer attest to each assignment, records the decision for auditors, and can remove eligibility automatically. Expiring eligibility removes access on a timer without anyone deciding that it is no longer needed and forces administrators to re-request it. A compliant-device condition changes how activation happens, not whether the eligibility continues. An access package is built for requesting and expiring access to apps, groups, and sites, and does not have the role owner attest to existing eligibility.

q: A release pipeline deletes and recreates 12 Function Apps on every deployment. All of them need to read secrets from the same Key Vault, and the team wants to grant that permission once and have it survive every recreation. What should you do?
opts: Create one user-assigned managed identity, attach it to all 12 apps, and grant it the Key Vault role once
Enable a system-assigned managed identity on one app and let the other eleven use that identity
Store a service principal secret in each app's settings and grant the principal the Key Vault role once
Enable a system-assigned managed identity on each app and have the pipeline re-grant the Key Vault role after each deployment
why: A user-assigned identity is a standalone resource: it can be attached to many apps and keeps its role assignment when the apps are deleted and recreated. A system-assigned identity is created and deleted with its app, so every recreation produces a new principal that needs the role granted again, which the pipeline would have to script. An app cannot borrow another app's system-assigned identity. A shared service principal secret works but brings back secret storage and rotation, which managed identities exist to avoid.

q: A policy must add a missing CostCenter tag, with a default value, to resources as they are created, and must also be able to fix the tag on thousands of existing resources through remediation. Creation must not be blocked, and no separate resource should be deployed. Which effect fits?
opts: Audit
DeployIfNotExists
Modify
Append
why: Modify adds or updates tags on the resource itself and, through a remediation task, can correct existing resources as well. Append also adds fields during a create or update request, but it only acts on those requests, cannot be remediated against existing resources, and Microsoft recommends Modify for tags. DeployIfNotExists deploys a separate related resource, which is not needed here. Audit only reports noncompliance.

q: Break-glass emergency access accounts should be synchronized from on-premises Active Directory, so their passwords follow the same policies as every other administrator account.
opts: True
False
why: Break-glass accounts should be cloud-only so that an on-premises outage, a sync failure, or a federation problem can never be what locks the organization out. Their protection comes from long, unique credentials stored securely and from monitoring and alerting on any sign-in, not from inheriting on-premises account policies.

q: Which two statements correctly distinguish Azure RBAC from Azure Policy? (Choose two.)
opts: Azure Policy can reject a deployment requested by a user who holds the Owner role on the subscription
A role assigned at a management group and a policy assigned there both apply to every subscription beneath it
Azure Policy decides by checking who the requesting user is, while RBAC checks the properties of the resource
Assigning an Azure Policy to a user gives that user permission to manage the resources in scope
A custom role definition can limit a Contributor to creating resources only in approved regions
why: Policy evaluates the properties of what is being deployed and applies to everyone at its scope, including Owners, and both RBAC role assignments and policy assignments inherit downward from a management group. RBAC cannot express a condition such as an allowed region, because a role definition lists operations, not resource properties. A policy never grants permissions to anyone, and the claim that Policy checks the user while RBAC checks resource properties has the two services reversed: RBAC checks who is acting, while Policy checks what is being created.

q: A managed service provider administers Azure subscriptions for 30 customers, each in its own Entra tenant. Engineers must sign in only with the provider's own identities and MFA, customers must keep ownership and be able to revoke access, and the provider wants one view across all subscriptions. What should you use?
opts: Cross-tenant synchronization to create member accounts for engineers in each customer tenant
Azure Lighthouse with delegated Azure RBAC roles for the provider's engineer groups
B2B guest accounts for each engineer in each customer tenant, with roles assigned per tenant
Transferring each customer subscription into the provider's tenant under one management group
why: Lighthouse lets engineers manage delegated subscriptions from their own tenant with their own identities and MFA, customers keep ownership and can remove the delegation, and the provider sees every customer in one view. B2B guests or synchronized member accounts need separate accounts and sign-in context in each of 30 tenants, and each customer's own policies apply to them. Moving subscriptions into the provider's tenant transfers control to the provider, which is exactly what the customers want to avoid.

q: A CISO wants a continuously updated measure of how well the company's Azure subscriptions follow security benchmark recommendations, such as open management ports and unencrypted storage, with prioritized fixes. The company has no need for a SIEM. Which service should provide it?
opts: Microsoft Defender for Cloud, using its Secure Score
Microsoft Sentinel, with analytics rules on subscription activity
The Azure Policy compliance dashboard for a built-in initiative
Microsoft Entra ID Protection risk detections
why: Defender for Cloud assesses resource configuration against security benchmarks, produces prioritized recommendations, and rolls them into a Secure Score tracked over time. Sentinel is a SIEM and SOAR that detects and responds to threats from collected logs, which the scenario says is not needed. The Policy compliance view reports pass or fail against policy rules but does not score or prioritize security posture. Entra ID Protection detects risky identities and sign-ins, not resource configuration.

q: A user assigned Owner on a storage account can read the blob contents when requests are authorized with Microsoft Entra ID, with no additional role assignment.
opts: True
False
why: Owner and Contributor grant control-plane Actions such as managing the account. Reading blob data through Entra authorization needs data-plane permissions (DataActions), usually through a role such as Storage Blob Data Reader or a custom role that lists DataActions. Control-plane roles can retrieve account keys, which is a separate path that bypasses Entra data authorization, and many designs disable shared-key access for exactly that reason.

q: Resource logs from 40 Azure resources in three regions must be forwarded in near real time to a third-party SIEM that is hosted outside Azure and reads from Kafka-compatible or event hub endpoints. The same logs must also be queryable in Azure. What should you recommend?
opts: An Azure Advisor export of the resource logs on a daily schedule
A diagnostic setting that sends the logs to a storage account, which the SIEM polls every hour
Azure Monitor Agent on each resource with a data collection rule that targets the SIEM
Diagnostic settings that send the logs to an event hub and to a Log Analytics workspace
why: A diagnostic setting can send the same data to several destinations, and an event hub is the streaming destination that external SIEMs consume, while the workspace serves queries in Azure. A storage account is an archive that the SIEM would poll with delay. Azure Monitor Agent collects guest data from machines and does not apply to platform resource logs. Advisor produces recommendations, not logs.

q: A security team ingests 2 TB per day of verbose firewall logs. They are rarely queried, but must be retained and searchable for 7 years for audits, and cost must be minimized. Which design is best?
opts: Delete the logs after 30 days and rely on Microsoft Defender for Cloud to keep the history
Put the table on a low-cost table plan and extend its total retention to seven years
Send the logs to Application Insights, which keeps all telemetry for seven years
Keep the table on the Analytics plan and set interactive retention to seven years
why: Table plans let rarely used, high-volume data sit on a cheaper plan, and total retention can be extended to up to 12 years, with older data retrieved by search jobs or queries as the plan allows. Keeping everything on the Analytics plan pays the full interactive price for data nobody queries. Application Insights has no seven-year guarantee, and Defender for Cloud does not keep your raw logs.

q: An AKS platform team already uses PromQL queries and Grafana dashboards. It wants to keep them for new Azure clusters without running and patching Prometheus servers or Grafana instances. Which services should you recommend?
opts: Azure Monitor managed Prometheus with Azure Managed Grafana
Application Insights with an availability test created for each pod
VM insights on each AKS node with the Dependency map switched on
Azure Service Health with a custom alert rule created per cluster
why: Managed Prometheus stores the metrics without servers to operate, and Managed Grafana hosts the dashboards, so existing PromQL and Grafana skills transfer. Application Insights targets application telemetry, not pod metrics. VM insights looks at nodes as VMs, not Kubernetes workloads, and Service Health reports on Azure platform incidents.

q: You are designing data collection for 300 Windows and Linux VMs, some Arc-enabled. Security events must go to one workspace, performance counters to another, and a noisy event ID must be dropped before storage to save cost. Which approach meets the requirements?
opts: Diagnostic settings on each VM resource that filter out the noisy event ID before storage
The legacy Log Analytics agent with a single workspace key configured on each machine
Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules that route sources and transform rows
A custom script on every VM that deletes the noisy events from the workspace afterwards
why: Azure Monitor Agent is the supported collector, and its data collection rules choose sources, destinations, and transformations, so different data can go to different workspaces and noisy rows can be dropped at ingestion. The legacy agent was retired in August 2024 and has no data collection rules. Diagnostic settings handle platform logs and not guest data, and deleting events afterwards means paying to ingest them first.

q: Users report intermittent failures in a checkout flow that spans a web front end, three microservices, and a SQL database. You need to see end-to-end transaction traces and the slowest dependency. Which solution should you recommend?
opts: Application Insights with distributed tracing across the services
VM insights with the Map feature enabled on all of the web servers
Azure Advisor performance recommendations reviewed for each service
Network Watcher connection monitor between each pair of services
why: Application Insights follows a request across services and dependencies, which shows where time is spent. VM insights shows machine performance and connections but no application transactions. Advisor gives configuration recommendations and not traces, and connection monitor measures network latency, which does not reveal which application dependency is slow.

q: VM1 stopped responding at 03:10. You need to know quickly whether the cause was an Azure platform event affecting that VM, such as a host failure, rather than something inside the guest. Which tool should you check first?
opts: Azure Policy compliance for the resource group
Log Analytics workspace usage and cost
Azure Advisor reliability recommendations
Resource Health for VM1
why: Resource Health reports the availability of an individual resource and whether a platform event, such as a host problem, affected it. Service Health is the subscription-wide view of incidents and maintenance. Advisor offers configuration suggestions, workspace usage is about cost, and Policy compliance does not report availability.

q: Remote employees must reach an on-premises intranet web application from the internet. Security forbids opening inbound ports and prefers authentication before any traffic reaches the datacenter, with Conditional Access applied. There is no VPN. What should you recommend?
opts: Microsoft Entra Domain Services with a secure LDAP endpoint
Microsoft Entra Application Proxy with a connector installed on-premises
A site-to-site VPN gateway and a public load balancer in front of the web servers
Azure Front Door with the on-premises servers as public origins
why: Application Proxy uses an outbound-only connector, preauthenticates through Microsoft Entra ID, and can apply Conditional Access, with no inbound ports. A VPN and public load balancer expose more and are not preauthenticated. Front Door would need the servers reachable publicly, and Domain Services provides legacy domain features, not web publishing.

q: A startup is designing a new consumer mobile app that needs sign-up, sign-in with social accounts, and self-service password reset, for an expected 30,000 monthly users. Which identity service should you recommend?
opts: Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration invitations for each user
Microsoft Entra Domain Services with a custom login page
Azure AD B2C in a newly created tenant
Microsoft Entra External ID configured for customers
why: External ID is the current customer identity offering and includes a free tier for the first 50,000 monthly active users. Azure AD B2C is no longer available for purchase by new customers, B2B invitations are for partner users in a workforce tenant, and Domain Services is not a consumer identity service.

q: When an employee joins, the company must automatically generate a temporary access pass and add the person to the right groups on the start date, and on the last day disable the account. Which capability should you use?
opts: Conditional Access with a sign-in frequency control
Privileged Identity Management with time-bound eligibility
Lifecycle workflows in Microsoft Entra ID Governance
Access reviews with auto-apply on a monthly schedule
why: Lifecycle workflows run tasks for joiners, movers, and leavers on triggers such as a start date or last day. Access reviews recertify existing access periodically. Conditional Access governs sign-in conditions, and PIM governs activation of privileged roles.

q: A data science team must read only the blobs that carry the tag Project=Cascade in a storage account that also holds data for other projects. You want to avoid creating a custom role or splitting the data into new accounts. What should you do?
opts: Apply a CanNotDelete lock on every blob that carries one of the other tags
Assign Reader on the storage account and hand out a SAS token for each blob
Create a lifecycle management rule that deletes blobs which have other tags
Assign Storage Blob Data Reader with a condition on the blob index tag
why: Azure ABAC adds a condition to a role assignment that checks attributes such as blob index tags, so the built-in role is narrowed without custom roles or new accounts. Reader is a control-plane role and SAS tokens per blob are unmanageable. Lifecycle rules and locks do not control who can read data.

q: Regulators require that the organization's encryption keys are held in a single-tenant, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSM that the organization fully controls, and the keys will protect storage accounts through customer-managed keys. Which service should you recommend?
opts: Azure Key Vault Premium with software-protected keys
Azure Key Vault Managed HSM
Azure Payment HSM
Azure Key Vault Standard
why: Managed HSM is the single-tenant, fully managed HSM service on FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated hardware, and it supports customer-managed keys for storage. Key Vault Standard keeps keys in software and Premium adds HSM protection in a multitenant service. Payment HSM serves payment PIN processing and is not a general service for storage encryption keys.

q: An application running on VMs uses PKCS#11 to talk to an HSM today. The team plans a lift and shift to Azure with minimal code changes and needs a single-tenant HSM with PKCS#11, JCA, and CNG support. Which service fits?
opts: Azure App Configuration
Azure Key Vault Standard
Azure Key Vault Managed HSM
Azure Cloud HSM
why: Azure Cloud HSM is the single-tenant service with full native PKCS#11, JCA/JCE, and CNG support for lift-and-shift applications. Managed HSM and Key Vault are accessed through the Key Vault APIs, which would need code changes, and App Configuration does not store keys.

q: Forty microservices read database connection strings and feature flags. Security requires secrets to live in a vault, developers want to toggle features without redeploying, and the same settings must vary by environment. Which combination should you recommend?
opts: Azure Policy parameters that every application reads when it starts up
A storage account table that holds the secrets and the flags in plain text
App Configuration with labels and Key Vault references, using managed identities
Environment variables that are baked into every one of the container images
why: App Configuration holds settings and feature flags centrally, uses labels per environment, references secrets in Key Vault so they are never stored in it, and lets applications refresh without redeploying. Baked-in variables require rebuilds, plain-text tables break the secrets requirement, and Policy parameters are governance inputs rather than runtime configuration.

q: A company must discover and classify sensitive data across Azure SQL, storage accounts, and on-premises file servers, and show data lineage to auditors. Which service should you recommend?
opts: Microsoft Purview
Azure Policy built-in initiatives
Microsoft Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance
Azure Resource Graph
why: Purview catalogs and classifies data across sources and tracks lineage. Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance reports whether resource configuration meets a standard, Resource Graph queries resource metadata, and Policy enforces rules on resource properties; none of them classifies the content of data.

q: Auditors ask you to show how the subscriptions currently measure up against the PCI DSS standard, with a list of failing controls and the resources involved. Which feature should you use?
opts: A Log Analytics workbook showing the VM count per region
A management group with a CanNotDelete lock on every subscription
The regulatory compliance dashboard in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
The Azure Advisor cost recommendations list
why: The regulatory compliance dashboard maps resource configuration to standards, including PCI DSS, through Azure Policy initiatives and lists failing controls with the affected resources. Resource counts, cost recommendations, and locks do not assess compliance with a standard.

q: Every resource in the subscription must automatically receive the CostCenter tag from its resource group when the tag is missing, without developers adding it to templates. What should you assign?
opts: A Deny policy that rejects any resource created without the CostCenter tag
A Modify policy that inherits the CostCenter tag from the resource group
A resource lock configured on each group to copy its tags to the resources
An Azure RBAC role that grants permission to write tags on all resources
why: Tags are not inherited automatically, and a Modify policy, such as the built-in inherit-a-tag-from-the-resource-group policy, adds the missing tag to resources. Deny would block deployments rather than fix them, RBAC governs who can write tags and not what gets written, and locks do not copy tags.

q: Which two statements about diagnostic settings are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: A destination can be an event hub, which is how data is streamed to an external SIEM
A diagnostic setting collects guest operating system logs from inside a VM
One diagnostic setting can send the same data to a workspace and to a storage account
A diagnostic setting is the only way to configure alert rules on metrics
why: A diagnostic setting routes platform resource logs and metrics to one or more destinations, including workspaces, storage accounts, event hubs, and partner solutions. Guest operating system data comes from Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule, and alert rules are separate resources from diagnostic settings.

q: Azure AD B2C remains available for new customers to purchase, so it is the recommended identity service for a new consumer app designed today.
opts: True
False
why: Effective May 1, 2025, Azure AD B2C is no longer available to purchase for new customers, so new consumer identity designs use Microsoft Entra External ID. Existing B2C tenants keep working.

q: A Log Analytics table's total retention can be extended well beyond its interactive retention, up to 12 years, so rarely used data can be kept at lower cost.
opts: True
False
why: Analytics retention keeps data fully available for interactive queries, and total retention can be extended to up to 12 years, with the older data in a low-cost state that is reached with search jobs for Analytics and Basic tables.

q: A financial firm is migrating an on-premises SQL Server instance with 12 databases that rely on SQL Agent jobs and cross-database queries. It wants Microsoft to own OS and engine patching and backups, and it will not rewrite the application. Which service should you recommend?
opts: Azure SQL Managed Instance
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale
Azure SQL Database elastic pool
SQL Server on an Azure VM with automated patching
why: Managed Instance offers near-complete SQL Server engine compatibility, including SQL Agent and cross-database queries, as fully managed PaaS where Microsoft handles OS patching, engine patching, and backups. An elastic pool shares resources among single databases that cannot run SQL Agent jobs or query across databases the way an instance can, and Hyperscale is a single-database service tier with the same limits. SQL Server on a VM with automated patching keeps the features, but the VM, its OS configuration, and its backups remain the customer's responsibility.

q: A messaging app uses a Cosmos DB account with multi-region writes. A user must always see their own just-posted messages after reloading, reads of other users' messages may lag, and the team wants the lowest latency and RU cost that still gives that guarantee. Which consistency level fits?
opts: Session
Bounded staleness
Strong
Eventual
why: Session consistency guarantees read-your-writes and monotonic reads within a client session while staying low-latency and cheap, which is exactly the stated need. Eventual is cheaper still but can return a stale view that omits a user's own post. Bounded staleness limits how stale reads can be for all clients, a stronger and costlier guarantee than needed. Strong is not supported on accounts with multiple write regions, and even where it is available it costs the most latency and RUs.

q: A Cosmos DB container stores IoT telemetry partitioned by deviceType, but 95% of devices share one type. Writes to that logical partition are throttled although most of the container's total RU/s goes unused. Dashboards almost always query one device's readings. What should you do?
opts: Raise the container's maximum autoscale RU/s so each partition receives more throughput
Migrate the data to a container partitioned by the device identifier
Migrate the data to a container partitioned by deviceType combined with the datacenter region
Migrate the data to a container partitioned by the ingestion timestamp
why: A partition key should have many distinct values and match the common query filter; the device identifier has high cardinality and lines up with per-device queries. A timestamp key is high-cardinality but monotonic, so every current write lands on the newest partition, which creates a different hot spot and scatters per-device queries across partitions. Combining deviceType with a region still yields only a handful of values, so the hot partition remains. More RU/s is divided among physical partitions, so the hot partition still hits its own per-partition limit.

q: A storage account must keep accepting writes without any failover if one datacenter in the primary region is lost. During a regional outage, a reporting app must be able to read the data from a second region without anyone initiating a failover. Which redundancy option should you select?
opts: Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) without read access
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) in the primary region
Read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS)
Read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS)
why: RA-GZRS keeps synchronous copies across three zones in the primary region, so losing a datacenter does not interrupt writes, and replicates asynchronously to a secondary region whose copy is readable at any time. RA-GRS keeps its primary-region copies in one datacenter, so losing it would interrupt writes until a failover. GZRS has the same zone resilience, but its secondary copy cannot be read until a failover occurs. ZRS has no secondary region at all.

q: A legal team keeps seven years of contract records in Blob storage. Each record is opened once or twice a year, and when an attorney asks for one it must open immediately, with no restore step. Storage cost should be as low as possible within that constraint. Which access tier should you use?
opts: Cold
Archive
Cool
Hot
why: Cold is the lowest-cost tier that is still online, so blobs open immediately, and its higher read cost and 90-day minimum suit records opened once or twice a year. Archive is cheaper to store, but blobs must be rehydrated before they can be read, which can take hours and rules out immediate access. Cool is also online, but it costs more to store than Cold and is aimed at data accessed somewhat more often. Hot has the highest storage cost and is meant for frequently accessed data.

q: A data engineering team runs Spark jobs over petabytes of semi-structured files. Each team needs ACLs at the directory and file level, and nightly jobs rename large folders, which must complete as a single atomic operation. Cost should stay low. Which storage solution fits?
opts: Azure Files Premium with an NFS share mounted on each Spark node
Azure NetApp Files with a large capacity pool and snapshots
Blob storage with a flat namespace and RBAC assigned per container
Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (a storage account with hierarchical namespace)
why: ADLS Gen2 is Blob storage with a hierarchical namespace, which provides POSIX-style ACLs on directories and files and atomic directory renames at lake scale, at Blob pricing. A flat namespace has no real directories, so renaming a folder means copying and deleting every blob, and RBAC applies at container scope or above rather than per file. Premium Azure Files and Azure NetApp Files are higher-cost file-share services, not lake-scale analytics storage with ACLs.

q: A team plans to move an on-premises SQL Server with 12 databases to Azure SQL Managed Instance, with minimal downtime at cutover. Which step should the team take FIRST?
opts: Take full backups of every database and restore them to the target with native restore
Assess the source databases for compatibility blockers, for example with Azure Migrate
Provision a Managed Instance sized to match the source server's CPU and memory
Start an online migration in Database Migration Service and fix errors as they appear
why: Assessment comes first because its findings decide whether Managed Instance is a viable target and how to size it; starting a migration before that risks discovering blockers in the middle of a cutover. Starting an online migration in DMS or restoring native backups are migration steps that follow once the target is validated. Provisioning a target to match source hardware guesses at size before real utilization and compatibility data exist.

q: In an Azure SQL auto-failover group, all databases in the group fail over together as a unit; one database cannot be failed over while the others stay on the original primary server.
opts: True
False
why: The failover group is the unit of failover: the listener endpoints move for every member database at once, which is what keeps a single connection string valid for the whole application. Failing over one database independently is something active geo-replication does outside a failover group.

q: With Session consistency in Cosmos DB, a user in one client session is guaranteed to immediately read a write that another user committed through a different client session.
opts: True
False
why: Session consistency guarantees read-your-writes and monotonic reads only within a single client session. A different session can see older data for a short time. Only Strong consistency guarantees that every client reads the latest committed write.

q: A storage account's default access tier can be set to Archive, so every new blob lands in the Archive tier automatically.
opts: True
False
why: Archive is not available as an account-level default. It is assigned per blob after upload, either manually or by a lifecycle management rule, which is why a design that needs data to age into Archive needs a lifecycle policy rather than a default setting.

q: Which two statements about Azure Storage redundancy are true? (Choose two.)
opts: In GZRS, the secondary region's copy is spread across the availability zones of that region
In GZRS, the secondary-region copy uses locally redundant storage rather than zone-redundant storage
In RA-GRS, the data in the secondary region becomes readable once a failover has been triggered by Microsoft or the customer
GRS keeps primary-region copies in one datacenter, while GZRS spreads them across availability zones
ZRS protects data against the loss of a whole Azure region as well as a single zone
why: GZRS is zone-redundant only in the primary region; its secondary-region copy is stored with LRS. GRS keeps its primary copies in a single datacenter, which is the difference GZRS adds. ZRS stays inside one region, so it cannot survive a regional loss, and RA-GRS exists precisely so that the secondary copy can be read before any failover.

q: Which two statements about Cosmos DB partition key design are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Cosmos DB spreads a single hot logical partition across physical partitions to share its load
A monotonically increasing key such as a timestamp tends to concentrate current writes on one partition
Choosing a key that appears in most query filters lets queries target a single partition instead of fanning out
The partition key value of an existing item can be updated in place with a replace operation
A key with only a few distinct values is acceptable because partitions rebalance automatically
why: Queries that include the partition key are routed to one partition, while those that do not fan out to every partition at higher cost and latency. A timestamp always increases, so all new writes land on the latest partition. An item's partition key value is immutable: changing it means deleting and recreating the item. A logical partition cannot be split across physical partitions, so Cosmos DB cannot relieve a hot logical partition, and automatic rebalancing moves whole logical partitions, not parts of one.

q: Application logs in Blob storage are read daily for 30 days, rarely until day 90, and never afterward, but must be kept seven years and then deleted. The team wants this handled automatically with the least administrative effort. What should you configure?
opts: A lifecycle management policy: Cool at 30 days, Archive at 90 days, delete at seven years
A timer-triggered Azure Function that scans the container daily and re-tiers or deletes blobs by age
A seven-year time-based immutability policy on the container, applied as soon as logs are written
Blob versioning enabled and the account's default access tier set to Cool for all new logs
why: A lifecycle management policy moves blobs between tiers and deletes them based on age with no code to run or maintain. A scheduled Function can reproduce that behavior but is custom code to write, monitor, and pay for. An immutability policy blocks modification and deletion; it neither moves data between tiers nor deletes anything when it expires. Versioning and a Cool default tier change where new blobs start, not how they age into Archive or when they are deleted.

q: A broker-dealer must store trade records so that nobody, including subscription Owners, can modify or delete them until a fixed seven-year period ends. Which configuration meets the requirement?
opts: A CanNotDelete resource lock on the storage account itself
A time-based retention policy on the container, then locked
A legal hold applied to the container until the period ends
A time-based retention policy on the container, left unlocked
why: A locked time-based retention policy provides write-once, read-many storage: nobody can modify or delete the blobs, and the retention cannot be shortened, until it expires, even with Owner rights. An unlocked policy is intended for testing; its settings can be changed or the policy removed. A legal hold blocks modification and deletion but has no fixed period and can be cleared by anyone with permission to do so. A CanNotDelete lock protects the storage account resource, not the blobs inside it, which can still be deleted through the data plane.

q: Which two statements about Azure Synapse serverless and dedicated SQL pools are true? (Choose two.)
opts: A serverless SQL pool bills for provisioned DWUs even during hours when the pool sits idle
A serverless SQL pool is the more economical choice for a heavy workload that runs around the clock
A dedicated SQL pool can be paused to stop compute charges, while its stored data continues to be billed
A serverless SQL pool can query files in the data lake, such as Parquet or CSV, without first loading them into tables
A dedicated SQL pool bills per terabyte of data processed by each query, instead of for provisioned compute
why: A dedicated pool's provisioned compute can be paused to stop compute charges while storage is still billed, and a serverless pool queries files in the lake directly with no loading step. The billing claims about serverless and dedicated pools are swapped in the other statements: serverless bills per data processed with nothing provisioned, and dedicated bills for provisioned DWUs. A constant heavy workload generally suits a dedicated pool better, since per-query billing adds up when the pool would otherwise be busy all day.

q: An application writes to a GRS storage account. The team wants a read-only reporting service to read from the secondary region during normal operation, with no other change to how data is replicated. What should they do?
opts: Keep GRS and give the reporting service a read-only SAS token for the primary endpoint
Enable read access to convert the account to RA-GRS, and point the reporting service at the account's secondary endpoint
Convert the account to GZRS, whose secondary-region copy is readable by default
Enable read access to convert the account to RA-GRS; the existing primary endpoint then serves reads from either region
why: Enabling read access converts GRS to RA-GRS and exposes the replicated copy at a separate secondary endpoint (the account name with a -secondary suffix), so the reporting code must be pointed at it and must tolerate slightly stale data because replication is asynchronous. The primary endpoint never redirects reads to the secondary. GZRS adds zone redundancy in the primary region, but its secondary copy is not readable unless read access (RA-GZRS) is enabled. A read-only SAS token limits permissions on the primary but does not read from the secondary.

q: An administrator deleted a container holding thousands of blobs. Blob soft delete was enabled on the account with a 14-day retention, yet the team cannot restore the container's contents. Which feature should have been enabled to make this recoverable?
opts: Container soft delete
A time-based immutability policy on the container
Blob versioning
The change feed
why: Blob soft delete protects individual blobs; deleting the whole container bypasses it. Container soft delete retains a deleted container and its blobs for a configurable window so they can be restored. Versioning keeps prior versions of each blob, but those versions are deleted along with the container. The change feed only logs changes and cannot restore anything. An immutability policy would have prevented the blobs from being deleted, but it does not make an already-deleted container recoverable.

q: A team is moving an existing app built on MongoDB drivers and aggregation queries to a fully managed, globally distributed database. It wants the fewest application code changes and no database servers to operate. Which should you choose?
opts: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, rewriting the data access layer to its SDK
MongoDB Community Edition on VMs in two regions with replica sets
Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB
Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server, storing documents as JSONB
why: Cosmos DB for MongoDB speaks the MongoDB wire protocol, so existing drivers and queries work with few changes, and it is a managed service with global distribution. Cosmos DB for NoSQL is the native API and a strong choice for new apps, but it means rewriting data access against a different query model. Storing documents as JSONB in PostgreSQL also needs a rewrite. MongoDB on VMs keeps the code but leaves replication, patching, and failover to the team.

q: A team migrates a PostgreSQL application and needs automatic failover if an entire availability zone fails, with no committed transactions lost. It must keep the PostgreSQL engine and minimize administration. What should you recommend?
opts: PostgreSQL on Azure VMs in two zones with streaming replication
Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server with zone-redundant high availability
Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server with a read replica in another zone, promoted manually
Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server with same-zone high availability
why: Zone-redundant high availability keeps a standby in another zone with synchronous replication, so committed transactions are not lost and failover is automatic, all managed by the service. Same-zone high availability also fails over automatically, but its standby shares the primary's zone and does not survive a zone failure. A read replica replicates asynchronously, so recent commits can be lost on promotion, and promotion is a manual step. Self-managed VM replication could be built to meet the targets but puts replication, patching, and failover orchestration on the team.

q: After a time-based retention policy on a blob container is locked, its retention period can still be extended, but it can no longer be shortened or removed.
opts: True
False
why: Locking makes the policy irreversible in the weakening direction: the interval can be increased but never decreased, and the policy cannot be removed. Extending is allowed because it only strengthens protection. This one-way behavior is what makes locked mode suitable for regulatory write-once, read-many requirements.

q: Which two statements correctly distinguish blob soft delete, legal holds, and locked retention policies? (Choose two.)
opts: A legal hold ends automatically when the container's retention interval elapses
A legal hold stays in effect until someone explicitly clears it, with no built-in expiry
Soft delete satisfies write-once, read-many requirements because deleted blobs can always be restored
A locked time-based retention policy can be shortened by an Owner after a formal approval process
Soft delete does not stop a user with delete permission from deleting a blob; it only keeps the deleted blob recoverable for a retention window
why: Soft delete is recovery-focused: deletion still happens, and the blob is restorable only for the retention window. A legal hold is open-ended; it persists until an authorized user clears it. A locked retention policy cannot be shortened by anyone, including an Owner. Soft delete does not meet write-once, read-many requirements because blobs can still be deleted and eventually expire from the recoverable state, and a legal hold has no connection to a retention interval.

q: A transactional Azure SQL Database of about 1.5 TB must stay available through the loss of a datacenter, with automatic failover and no data loss inside the region. The team also wants a read-only replica for reporting that is included without paying for extra compute. Which service tier should you recommend?
opts: The vCore model's General Purpose service tier, with zone redundancy
The DTU model's Premium tier, without zone redundancy
The vCore model's Business Critical service tier, with zone redundancy
The vCore model's Hyperscale service tier, with a named replica for reporting
why: Business Critical keeps several synchronously committed replicas on local SSD, and with zone redundancy they are spread across availability zones, so losing a datacenter fails over automatically with no data loss; one of those replicas is readable for reporting at no extra charge. General Purpose with zone redundancy also survives a zone loss, but it has no built-in readable replica, so reporting would need extra compute. A Hyperscale named replica is separate compute billed on top of the primary. A Premium database without zone redundancy keeps all its replicas in one datacenter, so losing that datacenter takes it down.

q: A new Cosmos DB workload in a single region needs roughly 2,000 RU/s for a few minutes, a few times a week, and is idle the rest of the time. The team wants no charge for provisioned capacity while idle. Which option fits?
opts: Autoscale provisioned throughput with a 4,000 RU/s maximum
Serverless capacity mode
Standard provisioned throughput of 2,000 RU/s with reserved capacity
Provisioned throughput lowered and raised by a scheduled Azure Function
why: Serverless bills only for the request units consumed, so idle time costs nothing, and this occasional peak fits within its limits. Autoscale never drops below 10% of its maximum, so a 4,000 RU/s maximum still bills at least 400 RU/s every hour. Standard provisioned throughput bills the full 2,000 RU/s around the clock, and a reservation discounts that without removing it. A scheduled function can lower provisioned throughput, but only down to the container's minimum, and it adds a component to maintain.

q: A serverless SQL pool query that scans a large CSV file in the data lake is billed for the data it processes, even if the query returns only a few rows.
opts: True
False
why: Serverless pricing is based on the amount of data a query processes, not on the size of its result. That is why columnar formats such as Parquet, where a query reads only the columns it needs, can cut cost sharply compared with scanning CSV, and why a constant heavy workload can be cheaper on a dedicated pool.

q: Which two statements about Cosmos DB capacity modes are true? (Choose two.)
opts: A serverless account can be configured with multi-region writes
Autoscale provisioned throughput stops billing completely whenever a container is idle
A serverless container has an upper limit on total storage that a provisioned-throughput container does not have
Autoscale provisioned throughput bills for at least 10% of its configured maximum RU/s, even when no requests arrive
Serverless capacity mode is the better choice for sustained heavy traffic that needs predictable performance
why: Autoscale scales between 10% of its maximum and the maximum, so an idle container still bills for that floor, and serverless containers have a storage cap that provisioned containers do not. Sustained, heavy, predictable traffic suits provisioned throughput rather than serverless, serverless is not available with multi-region writes, and autoscale never bills zero.

q: A bank stores national ID numbers in an Azure SQL Database. Database administrators and Microsoft operators must not be able to read the plaintext values, yet an application must still query them with equality comparisons. Which feature should you recommend?
opts: Transparent data encryption with a customer-managed key in Azure Key Vault
Always Encrypted, with the keys held in Azure Key Vault and used only by the client driver
Dynamic data masking on the column for all non-administrative users
Row-level security that filters rows by the signed-in user
why: Always Encrypted encrypts the column on the client, so the database engine and its administrators only ever see ciphertext, while deterministic encryption allows equality lookups. TDE encrypts files at rest but the engine and administrators still read plaintext. Dynamic data masking only changes what query results display and does not stop privileged users, and row-level security restricts rows rather than hiding column values.

q: Call-center agents query a customer table and must see only the last four digits of each credit card number, while the billing team sees the full number. The data must remain unchanged in storage. What should you configure?
opts: A separate copy of the table where the card numbers are truncated by a nightly job
Always Encrypted on the card column with keys given only to the billing team
Transparent data encryption with separate keys for the two teams
Dynamic data masking on the card column, with the billing team granted the UNMASK permission
why: Dynamic data masking changes what queries return for users without UNMASK, leaving stored data untouched, and it is simple to apply. Always Encrypted would also hide the value from agents but needs client driver changes and does not offer partial display. TDE has one key per database, not per team, and a nightly truncated copy is stale and doubles the data to manage.

q: An auditor must be able to prove that rows in a financial table were not altered after they were written, even by a database administrator. Which Azure SQL feature should you recommend?
opts: Row-level security that blocks updates for administrators
Ledger tables, with digests stored in a tamper-resistant location
Dynamic data masking on every financial column
Point-in-time restore with a seven-day retention
why: Ledger makes data changes tamper-evident by chaining cryptographic hashes into digests that can be verified later, and the digests can be stored outside the database's control. Masking affects display, row-level security can be altered by someone with enough privilege, and point-in-time restore recovers earlier states but does not prove that nothing was altered.

q: An OLTP database of 70 TB must stay on T-SQL. A reporting team needs several read-only replicas with their own compute size, isolated from the transactional workload, and backups must not slow the primary. Which design should you recommend?
opts: Azure SQL Database Hyperscale with named replicas for the reporting workload
Azure SQL Database Business Critical with the built-in readable secondary
A General Purpose database with five geo-replicas in other regions
Azure SQL Managed Instance General Purpose with an elastic pool of replicas
why: Hyperscale supports databases up to 128 TB, takes snapshot-based backups that do not load compute, and offers up to 30 named replicas, each with independently chosen compute for workload isolation. Business Critical has far lower size limits and only a built-in secondary. General Purpose cannot hold 70 TB, and elastic pools are not replicas of a single database.

q: A development team's Azure SQL Database is used for a few hours on weekdays and is idle overnight and at weekends. Cost must be minimized, and a short delay on the first connection after idle time is acceptable. Which configuration should you recommend?
opts: Hyperscale with the maximum number of named replicas
A DTU Premium database with reserved capacity
General Purpose serverless compute with auto-pause enabled
Business Critical provisioned compute with the smallest vCore count
why: Serverless scales compute with usage, bills per second, and can pause when idle so that only storage is billed, and the first connection after a pause resumes the database after a delay. The other options bill for provisioned resources around the clock, and replicas or reservations add cost instead of removing it.

q: A SaaS provider hosts 250 small Azure SQL databases, one per tenant. Each is busy at different times of the day, and per-database sizing wastes money. Which design provides the lowest cost without code changes?
opts: Place the databases in an elastic pool sized for the combined peak
Move every tenant database to its own SQL Server on a virtual machine
Merge all tenants into one Hyperscale database and filter by tenant ID
Give every database a Business Critical provisioned size for its own peak
why: An elastic pool lets databases share vCores or eDTUs, so tenants peaking at different times use the same pool without each being sized for its own peak. Merging tenants changes the application and the isolation model. Sizing each database for its peak is what wastes money, and a VM per tenant adds administration and cost.

q: A company runs SQL Server 2022 on-premises. It wants near real-time replication to Azure SQL Managed Instance to run reporting there now, to migrate with minimal downtime later, and to be able to fail back to on-premises if needed. Which feature should you recommend?
opts: Azure Database Migration Service in offline mode
Transactional replication with a distribution database on the managed instance
Log shipping to Azure Blob Storage with manual restore
The Managed Instance link feature
why: The link uses distributed availability groups to replicate in near real time between SQL Server and Managed Instance, allows read-only offloading and migration, and with SQL Server 2022 supports failing back. Offline migration service runs are not continuous, and log shipping and transactional replication do not offer the same managed failover and failback.

q: A retrieval-augmented generation application stores product documents as JSON in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL and needs similarity search over embeddings. The team wants to avoid running and syncing a separate vector database. What should you recommend?
opts: Move the documents to Azure SQL Database and use Always Encrypted for similarity
Store the embeddings in the same containers and use Cosmos DB vector search with a DiskANN index
Export the documents to Azure Files and search them with grep from an AKS job
Copy the embeddings nightly into Azure Table Storage and query them there
why: Cosmos DB for NoSQL supports vector embeddings next to the documents and similarity queries with flat, quantized flat, or DiskANN indexes, so no second system has to be kept in sync. Table Storage has no vector search, file search with grep does not scale, and Always Encrypted is a protection feature and not a similarity feature.

q: A lift-and-shift of a Linux high-performance application requires NFS 4.1 volumes with very low latency, snapshots, and cross-region replication. The team wants a fully managed first-party service rather than building NFS servers on VMs. Which service should you recommend?
opts: Azure Elastic SAN volumes exposed over iSCSI
Azure Blob Storage with the NFS 3.0 endpoint
Azure Files with a Standard HDD share
Azure NetApp Files
why: Azure NetApp Files provides managed NFS and SMB volumes with high performance, snapshots, and cross-region replication. The NFS endpoint of Blob Storage is for object workloads and has different semantics. Elastic SAN is block storage over iSCSI, not a file system, and a Standard HDD Azure Files share cannot meet very low latency.

q: A platform team runs 60 VMs and an AKS cluster, each with block storage needs that change often. They want to buy and manage one pool of capacity, IOPS, and throughput that all workloads attach to over iSCSI, rather than sizing 100 separate disks. Which service fits?
opts: Azure Files Premium shares
Azure Blob Storage with hierarchical namespace
Azure Elastic SAN
Azure Premium SSD v2 managed disks
why: Elastic SAN is a pooled block storage service whose volumes attach to many compute resources over iSCSI, and capacity and performance are scaled for the SAN as a whole. Managed disks are sized and billed individually, Azure Files exposes file shares, and Blob Storage is object storage.

q: A company wants one SaaS platform for data engineering, a lakehouse, warehousing, real-time analytics, and Power BI reporting, with all data stored in one logical lake in open format and little infrastructure to manage. Which service should you recommend?
opts: Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pool only
Azure SQL Managed Instance with SSIS packages
Azure HDInsight clusters with Data Lake Storage Gen2
Microsoft Fabric with OneLake
why: Fabric unifies those workloads in one SaaS experience on OneLake, which stores data in open Delta Parquet format. A dedicated SQL pool covers only warehousing, HDInsight is cluster-based and needs infrastructure management, and Managed Instance with SSIS covers relational and ETL needs but not the lakehouse and real-time parts.

q: Telemetry from 50,000 devices arrives at Azure Event Hubs. You need continuous SQL-like queries with five-minute tumbling windows that write aggregates to Azure SQL Database, with no servers to manage. Which service should you recommend?
opts: Azure Batch with a pool of low-priority nodes
Azure Stream Analytics
Azure Data Factory with a tumbling window trigger
An Azure Functions timer trigger that polls the event hub
why: Stream Analytics is a managed engine for continuous queries with window functions over Event Hubs or IoT Hub streams and supports Azure SQL Database outputs. Data Factory schedules batch pipelines, a polling function must be coded and scaled by you, and Batch runs parallel compute jobs rather than streaming queries.

q: A company will store about 200 TB of hot block blob data for the next three years, with a steady footprint. It wants to lower the cost per terabyte without changing the application or the redundancy. What should you do?
opts: Switch the account's redundancy setting from LRS to GRS
Enable blob versioning with a retention rule for older versions
Move all of the data to the Archive tier with a lifecycle rule
Purchase Azure Storage reserved capacity for a three-year term
why: Reserved capacity discounts a committed amount of storage for one or three years and suits a steady footprint, with no application change. Archive makes hot data unreadable until rehydrated, GRS raises the cost, and versioning keeps additional copies, which increases it.

q: Archive documents must be protected against the loss of an entire Azure region with the highest durability available for Azure Storage, and read access during a regional outage without waiting for a failover is not required. Which redundancy option is the most cost-effective choice that meets the requirement?
opts: Locally redundant storage
Zone-redundant storage
Geo-redundant storage
Read-access geo-zone-redundant storage
why: Geo-redundant storage replicates data to a secondary region and offers at least 16 nines of durability, which satisfies protection against a regional loss. The read-access geo-zone variant costs more and adds capabilities that were not requested. ZRS and LRS keep all copies in one region.

q: Which two statements about the Azure SQL Database Hyperscale service tier are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: It is available in the DTU-based purchasing model as well as vCore
It supports up to 30 named replicas, each with its own compute size
Backups are taken by copying the whole database from the primary compute node
It supports databases up to 128 TB with storage that grows automatically
why: Hyperscale offers named replicas for isolated read workloads and storage that scales automatically to 128 TB. It is available only in the vCore model, and its backups use storage snapshots that do not burden the compute node.

q: Transparent data encryption protects the data of an Azure SQL Database from a database administrator who queries the tables, because the data is encrypted for them.
opts: True
False
why: Transparent data encryption protects data at rest in files and backups and is decrypted transparently for authorized sessions, so an administrator who can query the tables sees plaintext. Always Encrypted is the feature that hides values from administrators.

q: Azure NetApp Files can present the same data over NFS and SMB in dual-protocol volumes.
opts: True
False
why: Azure NetApp Files supports NFS, SMB, and dual-protocol volumes, which makes it suitable for workloads that need the same files from Linux and Windows clients.

q: A three-tier VM application must be running in the paired region within one hour of a regional outage, losing no more than 15 minutes of data, with the tiers starting in the correct order. Which service should the design use?
opts: Azure Backup with cross-region restore on a GRS vault
Disk snapshots copied to the paired region by a scheduled script
VMs spread across availability zones in the primary region
Azure Site Recovery replication with an ordered recovery plan
why: Site Recovery continuously replicates the VMs to the paired region, giving an RPO of minutes, and a recovery plan starts the tiers in order, which meets both targets. Azure Backup with cross-region restore can restore into the paired region, but the RPO is the backup interval and restoring every VM takes far longer than failing over. Availability zones protect against datacenter loss, not a regional outage. Script-copied snapshots have no tier ordering or failover orchestration, and their RPO depends on the script schedule.

q: A line-of-business VM application must stay online if a single datacenter in its region fails, and must be recoverable in another region, with up to 15 minutes of data loss, if the whole region is lost. Which design meets both requirements?
opts: VMs in an availability set, replicated to a secondary region with Azure Site Recovery
VMs spread across availability zones, replicated to a secondary region with Azure Site Recovery
VMs spread across availability zones, backed up daily with Azure Backup to a GRS vault
VMs in one availability zone, replicated to a different zone in the same region with Azure Site Recovery
why: Spreading the VMs across availability zones keeps the tier running when one datacenter fails, and Site Recovery replicates continuously to another region, giving an RPO of minutes if the whole region is lost. An availability set stays inside one datacenter, so losing that datacenter takes the tier down. A daily backup allows up to a day of data loss, far beyond 15 minutes. Zone-to-zone replication keeps the data in the same region, so a regional loss still takes everything down.

q: An app uses 40 databases on one Azure SQL logical server and a fixed connection string. After a regional outage, all 40 databases must fail over together to a secondary region with no application change. What should you configure?
opts: An auto-failover group, with the read-write listener endpoint in the connection string
Geo-restore of each database from geo-redundant backups into the secondary region
Zone-redundant configuration for each database in the primary region
Active geo-replication on each database, failing over each one individually
why: An auto-failover group fails every database in the group over together and keeps the read-write listener endpoint stable, so the fixed connection string keeps working. Active geo-replication fails over per database, and each failover changes which server is primary, so connection strings would have to change or be managed database by database. Geo-restore rebuilds each database from backups on a different server, which takes much longer and also changes the server name. Zone redundancy only protects against a datacenter loss inside the primary region.

q: A reporting application must be running again within 4 hours of a regional outage and lose no more than 15 minutes of data. The business wants the lowest cost that meets both targets. Which design should you choose?
opts: Keep a hot standby copy of every VM running continuously in the secondary region, with manual failover
Replicate the VMs to the secondary region with Site Recovery, leaving recovery compute unprovisioned until a failover
Back up the VMs hourly to a GRS vault and restore them in the secondary region after an outage
