Run the full application in both regions behind Front Door, with a globally replicated database
why: Site Recovery replicates continuously, giving an RPO of minutes, and bills only for replication and storage until a failover starts the VMs; recovery within a few hours satisfies a 4-hour RTO, so this is the cheapest design that hits both numbers. Running everything in both regions is the fastest but by far the most expensive, and the RTO does not need it. Hourly backups meet the RTO but can lose up to an hour of data, missing the 15-minute RPO. A hot standby meets both targets but pays for full compute in the second region around the clock, which the cost requirement rules out.

q: A global app must keep serving users with no failover delay when a region fails, and users must be able to write data in their nearest region. Which design meets both requirements?
opts: Traffic Manager weighted routing to two regions, with an Azure SQL read replica in the second region
Front Door with priority routing to a standby region, with an Azure SQL auto-failover group
Front Door routing to two active regions, with a GRS-replicated storage account as the data tier
Front Door routing to two active regions, with a Cosmos DB account that has multi-region writes
why: Front Door can send traffic to two active regions at once, and Cosmos DB with multi-region writes accepts writes in each region, so a regional failure simply removes one active region and no failover step is needed. Priority routing to a standby region with a failover group is active-passive, so recovery takes time. A read replica keeps a single writer, so users far from it still write across regions, and Traffic Manager adds DNS-cache delay. A GRS storage account accepts writes only in its primary region, so the data tier is not active-active.

q: If a file is deleted inside a VM protected by Azure Site Recovery, the deletion is replicated to the secondary region as well, so Site Recovery replication is not a substitute for backup.
opts: True
False
why: Site Recovery replicates changes continuously, including deletions and corruption, and its recovery points are short-lived points meant for failover. Restoring an accidentally deleted file, or keeping monthly and yearly restore points, is a job for Azure Backup.

q: Because Azure Site Recovery replicates continuously, it can guarantee an RPO of zero when a VM fails over to the secondary region.
opts: True
False
why: Replication to another region is asynchronous, so the most recent writes may not have reached the target when the primary fails. Site Recovery typically achieves an RPO of seconds to minutes. A design that truly requires zero data loss needs synchronous replication, which is practical only between nearby locations such as availability zones in one region.

q: Which two statements correctly distinguish Azure Backup from Azure Site Recovery? (Choose two.)
opts: Site Recovery can restore an individual file from a protected VM to an earlier point in time
Azure Backup supports long-term retention, such as monthly and yearly restore points, while Site Recovery recovery points are short-lived
Azure Backup can restore a single file from a VM backup without restoring the whole VM
A Recovery Services vault holds either Backup items or Site Recovery items, not both
Azure Backup can run an ordered recovery plan that fails over each tier of an application in turn
why: Backup is built for point-in-time restores, including single-file recovery and retention measured in months or years, while Site Recovery keeps short-lived recovery points for failover. Site Recovery does not offer file-level restore, and the ordered recovery plan belongs to Site Recovery, not Backup. A single Recovery Services vault can hold both Backup and Site Recovery items.

q: Which two statements correctly apply RTO and RPO to a design? (Choose two.)
opts: RTO measures how much data is lost, while RPO measures how long the application is unavailable
Tightening the RPO automatically shortens the RTO, because both depend on replication frequency
A design that replicates every 15 minutes cannot meet a 5-minute RPO, however quickly it fails over
A design with an RPO of zero can still miss a 10-minute RTO if failover takes an hour
The RPO is determined by how long the failover process takes to complete
why: RPO is about how fresh the recovered data is, so a 15-minute replication interval cannot meet a 5-minute RPO whatever the failover speed, and RTO is about how long recovery takes, so zero data loss does not rescue a slow failover. The two objectives are independent, so tightening one does not shorten the other, and the definitions are reversed in the other statements: RPO limits data loss, RTO limits downtime.

q: Contoso backs up production VMs, which must remain restorable if a whole region is lost, and dev/test VMs, which only need protection from disk or rack failures at the lowest cost. How should the Recovery Services vaults be configured?
opts: Production vault on GRS; dev/test vault on GRS to keep one standard
Production vault on ZRS; dev/test vault on LRS
Production vault on GRS; dev/test vault on LRS
Both vaults on ZRS, since zone redundancy covers a regional outage
why: A vault's redundancy decides what survives: GRS keeps a copy of the backup data in the paired region, which production needs, while LRS is the cheapest option and still covers disk and rack failures, which is all dev/test needs. ZRS survives a zone loss but stays inside one region, so a regional loss still destroys it; zone redundancy does not cover a regional outage. GRS for dev/test would work but pays for geo-replication nobody asked for.

q: A Recovery Services vault used to back up an Azure VM must be in the same region as the VM, even when the vault's storage redundancy is GRS.
opts: True
False
why: Azure Backup requires the vault and the protected VM to share a region; GRS keeps a secondary copy of the backup data in the paired region but does not relocate the vault. This is why one central vault cannot back up VMs from several regions, and one vault per region is needed.

q: Production VM backups go to a GRS Recovery Services vault. In an annual DR drill, the team wants to restore VMs from the backups into the paired region on demand, without waiting for Microsoft to declare a regional disaster. What should you do?
opts: Switch the vault's storage redundancy to ZRS
Create a second vault in the paired region and register the same VMs with it
Enable Cross Region Restore on the vault
Enable Azure Site Recovery replication for each VM
why: Cross Region Restore lets you restore from the secondary-region copy of a GRS vault on demand, including for drills. A vault must be in the same region as the VMs it protects, so a second vault in the paired region cannot back up those VMs. ZRS is a different scope, zones within one region, and gives up the secondary-region copy altogether. Site Recovery replication would add failover capability, but it is not a way to restore from the existing backups, which is what the drill is meant to validate.

q: A payments platform needs an RTO under two minutes and can afford infrastructure in two regions, but its data layer cannot safely accept concurrent writes in two regions without risking double-processed payments. Which topology best fits?
opts: A single region with availability zones, accepting the risk of a regional outage
Pilot light: the replicated database runs in the second region, and the app tier starts after a failure
Warm standby: the app tier runs in the second region and its replicated database is promoted on failure
Active-active, with both regions accepting writes behind a global load balancer
why: A warm standby keeps the application tier running in the second region and promotes a replicated database on failure, so only one region ever accepts writes, which avoids double-processed payments, and the running app tier lets recovery fit a two-minute RTO. Active-active would reintroduce the concurrent-write conflict the scenario rules out. A pilot light starts the app tier only after a failure, and that start-up time would exceed a two-minute RTO. A single region with zones does not survive a regional outage.

q: A two-VM application tier must survive a single-rack power failure and Azure's planned host maintenance without both VMs going offline. The VMs exchange synchronous traffic, so the business wants both to stay in one datacenter. What is the simplest configuration that fits?
opts: Place both VMs on a single Azure Dedicated Host for isolation
Place both VMs in a proximity placement group to keep them physically close
Place the VMs in different availability zones of the same region
Place both VMs in an availability set, spread across fault and update domains
why: An availability set spreads VMs over fault domains (separate racks with independent power and network) and update domains (staggered maintenance reboots) inside one datacenter. Availability zones would protect against both failures, but they place the VMs in different datacenters, which the business ruled out. A proximity placement group does the opposite of spreading: it packs VMs close together for latency and offers no rack-level resilience. A single dedicated host is one physical machine, so a host failure or maintenance event takes both VMs down.

q: A single-region application depends on a web tier (App Service, 99.95% SLA) and a database (Azure SQL Database, 99.99% SLA), with no redundant paths. The business requires 99.95% availability end to end. What is the composite SLA, and does the design meet the requirement?
opts: About 99.94%, which falls just short of the requirement
99.99%, because the database's higher SLA covers gaps in the web tier
About 99.97%, because the two SLAs are averaged
99.95%, because the lowest SLA in the chain sets the composite
why: Dependencies in series multiply: 0.9995 x 0.9999 is about 0.99940, or 99.94%, which is below 99.95%. Adding a redundant path, such as a second region behind Front Door, is how a design recovers the gap. Taking the lowest SLA ignores the extra failure risk of the second dependency, a higher SLA never compensates for a weaker one in series, and SLAs are multiplied, not averaged.

q: Azure Site Recovery can replicate Azure VMs from one availability zone to another in the same region, not only to a different region.
opts: True
False
why: Zone-to-zone disaster recovery is supported for Azure VMs in regions that have availability zones. It protects against the loss of a zone while keeping data inside the region, so it does not protect against a regional outage; that still requires replication to a secondary region.

q: Regulations require monthly restore points for seven years but only 30 days of daily restore points. Which two statements about configuring this in Azure Backup are true? (Choose two.)
opts: One backup policy can combine 30 days of daily retention with 84 months of monthly retention
Each retention tier needs its own Recovery Services vault so the policies do not conflict
Monthly and yearly restore points are existing scheduled backups that are kept longer, not extra backup jobs
Setting the daily retention to 84 months keeps the same restore points as the monthly rule at lower cost
Site Recovery recovery points can be retained for seven years to cover the monthly requirement
why: Daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly retention are configured independently on one policy, and the longer-term points are simply selected scheduled backups that are retained longer, which is how the grandfather-father-son pattern keeps long reach at low cost. Retaining every daily point for 84 months would store far more data than the monthly rule. Site Recovery recovery points are short-lived and not meant for multi-year retention, and retention tiers do not need separate vaults.

q: Which two statements about availability sets are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Fault domains group VMs that share power and network hardware, so spreading VMs across them limits hardware-failure impact
An availability set can span several datacenters, so it survives the loss of one datacenter
Update domains group VMs that share a rack, power source, and network switch
During planned maintenance, Azure restarts one update domain at a time
A VM can belong to an availability set and an availability zone at the same time
why: Fault domains are the hardware boundary (shared rack, power, and network), and update domains stagger planned-maintenance reboots one group at a time. Update domains are not hardware groupings, so the rack, power, and switch description belongs to fault domains. An availability set lives within a single datacenter, and a VM is placed either in an availability set or in an availability zone, not both.

q: A team has already implemented availability zones, a secondary region, and automated failover for a critical workload. It now wants to see how the running production architecture behaves when a dependency becomes slow or a VM is killed, rather than trusting the design on paper. Which service should it use?
opts: Azure Chaos Studio
Application Insights availability tests
Azure Site Recovery test failover
Azure Load Testing
why: Chaos Studio injects faults, such as killing a VM or adding latency to a dependency, into a running environment so the team can observe how the real architecture responds. Site Recovery test failover validates that replicated VMs are recoverable, not how a live system tolerates faults. Load Testing generates traffic to measure performance under load and does not simulate component failure. Availability tests probe whether an endpoint responds, so they detect an outage but do not cause one to see how the system copes.

q: A Cosmos DB account has multi-region writes enabled in East US, West Europe, and Southeast Asia. East US becomes unavailable. What happens to write traffic?
opts: A failover priority list promotes one remaining region to be the sole write region after a delay
Writes stop until an administrator manually starts a failover
Writes continue in the other two regions, and the SDK redirects the app using its preferred regions list
The remaining regions become read-only until East US recovers, to avoid write conflicts
why: With multi-region writes every region already accepts writes, so no promotion is needed: the remaining regions keep serving writes, and the SDK sends requests to the next region in the app's preferred regions list. A failover priority list matters for accounts with a single write region. Waiting for a manual failover or turning regions read-only would defeat the availability benefit of multi-region writes.

q: After a customer-managed (account) failover of a GRS storage account, the newly promoted primary region is automatically GRS-protected again, with no further configuration needed.
opts: True
False
why: Immediately after an account failover, the storage account becomes locally redundant in its new primary region until an administrator explicitly reconfigures geo-redundancy — that protection isn't restored automatically on its own.

q: A SQL Server VM replicated with Site Recovery must fail over after a regional outage. The team would rather lose a few more minutes of data than start the database from a state captured mid-transaction. Which recovery point should they select when failing over?
opts: Latest, which processes all data sent to Site Recovery for the lowest RPO
Latest app-consistent, captured with the application quiesced
A custom recovery point chosen from the crash-consistent points
Latest processed, which gives the lowest RTO
why: The latest app-consistent point is the most recent one captured with the application quiesced, so no transaction is cut in half; the cost is a slightly older point because these are captured less often. Latest prioritizes the lowest RPO by processing everything received, but it does not guarantee application consistency. Latest processed prioritizes the lowest RTO by using the newest point already processed, again without that guarantee. A crash-consistent point captures the disk as if power had been lost, which is the mid-transaction risk the team wants to avoid.

q: A company uses Traffic Manager to (1) send traffic to a disaster recovery region only when the primary region fails, and (2) keep European users on European endpoints for data-residency reasons. Which two routing methods meet these needs? (Choose two.)
opts: Weighted routing
Geographic routing
Performance routing
Priority routing
MultiValue routing
why: Priority routing sends traffic to the primary endpoint and moves to the next only when the first fails, which is the DNS-layer pattern for active-passive disaster recovery, and Geographic routing maps each user's location to defined endpoints, which is how data-residency rules are enforced. Performance routing picks the lowest-latency endpoint, which could send a European user to a non-European endpoint. Weighted routing splits traffic by ratio, and MultiValue returns several healthy IP addresses; neither expresses failover order or residency.

q: A company stores 80 TB of business-critical documents in a Blob Storage account. Requirements: protect against accidental deletion of the whole storage account and against a malicious administrator, with a copy held outside the account. Which backup option should you recommend?
opts: Blob versioning combined with a lifecycle management rule
Vaulted backup of the blobs to a Backup vault
Operational backup with point-in-time restore on the same account
Blob soft delete with a 365-day retention period
why: Vaulted backup copies the data to a Backup vault in a separate, Microsoft-managed location, so it survives the deletion of the storage account. Operational backup, soft delete, and versioning all keep their data in the source account, so deleting the account removes them too, and lifecycle rules only move or delete data.

q: An Azure SQL Database must support restoring to any point in the last 14 days after user errors, and auditors require that the first full backup of each year is kept for 7 years. What should you configure?
opts: Geo-replication to a second region, with the replica delayed by 14 days
Point-in-time restore retention of 7 years, with no long-term retention configured
An Azure Backup vault policy for the database with seven-year retention
PITR retention of 14 days plus long-term retention for yearly backups of 7 years
why: Point-in-time restore retention is configurable from 1 to 35 days and covers the 14-day need, while long-term retention keeps selected full backups, such as a yearly one, for up to 10 years. PITR cannot be set to 7 years, geo-replication has no delay setting and is for availability, and Azure SQL Database backups are handled by the built-in features rather than a vault policy.

q: An Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account must allow restoring a container to any second within the last 25 days after an accidental deletion. Which backup configuration meets the requirement at the lowest retention that satisfies it?
opts: A Backup vault policy with daily recovery points
Continuous backup with the 30-day tier
Continuous backup with the 7-day tier
Periodic backup with the default interval and retention
why: Continuous backup supports point-in-time restore to any timestamp within the retention tier, and the 30-day tier covers 25 days. The 7-day tier is too short. Periodic backup restores only to the stored snapshots, not to any second, and Cosmos DB is not protected by a Backup vault policy.

q: Security wants assurance that even a compromised Global Administrator or backup administrator cannot disable immutability or delete recovery points in a Recovery Services vault before retention ends. What should you configure?
opts: Enable the immutable vault setting and lock it so it cannot be reversed
Move the vault to a different resource group with a restricted RBAC assignment
Enable soft delete with the default 14-day retention only
Apply a CanNotDelete resource lock on the vault
why: A locked immutable vault blocks operations that would lose recovery points and cannot be switched off, even by a privileged administrator. Soft delete alone can be disabled or changed, a resource lock can be removed by anyone with permission to delete locks, and moving the vault does not stop an administrator from acting on it.

q: Deleting a protected item or disabling protection in a Recovery Services vault must require approval from a separate security team that the backup administrators cannot override. Which feature should you use?
opts: Cross Region Restore enabled on the vault
A budget alert that notifies the security team of vault changes
Multi-user authorization with a Resource Guard owned by the security team
A custom Azure RBAC role that removes delete permissions from backup administrators
why: Multi-user authorization protects critical operations with a Resource Guard that lives under the security team's control, so a second approval is needed. A custom role can be reassigned by whoever manages access, a budget alert has no relation to vault operations, and Cross Region Restore is a recovery feature in a secondary region.

q: A company runs 120 on-premises VMware VMs. It has no secondary datacenter and needs a disaster recovery solution with an RTO of 30 minutes and an RPO of a few minutes, using Azure as the recovery site, with a tested plan that starts the database tier before the web tier. What should you recommend?
opts: Azure Site Recovery with a replication appliance and recovery plans
Azure Migrate with a one-time replication and cutover
Azure Backup with the MARS agent installed in each VM
Azure Storage account with object replication enabled
why: Site Recovery continuously replicates VMware VMs to Azure and uses recovery plans to order tiers and run test failovers. Azure Backup restores from copies and would not meet a 30-minute RTO for 120 VMs, Azure Migrate is for a one-time move, and object replication is a blob feature.

q: A critical Azure SQL Database must keep running through the loss of a single availability zone, with automatic failover and no change to the application's connection string and no data loss, but the company does not need protection from a regional outage. What should you choose?
opts: Place the database in an elastic pool with a higher vCore count
Schedule a nightly export of the database to a geo-redundant storage account
Configure an auto-failover group with a secondary in the paired region
Enable zone redundancy on the Business Critical or General Purpose database
why: Zone redundancy keeps replicas or storage across zones in the same region and fails over automatically with the same connection endpoint. A failover group protects against a regional outage and involves another region, which was not requested. Exports are manual recovery, and a bigger pool adds capacity but no zone resilience.

q: An Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server already uses zone-redundant high availability. The business now requires that if the entire primary region is lost, the database can be writable in another region within minutes, and losing a few minutes of recent data is acceptable. What should you add?
opts: A cross-region read replica that is promoted to a standalone server during a regional outage
Geo-redundant backup storage, with a geo-restore into the paired region after an outage
Nothing further, because zone-redundant high availability also fails over to the paired region
A longer point-in-time restore retention period, so the database can be rebuilt after the outage
why: A cross-region read replica is updated asynchronously, typically within seconds to a few minutes of the primary, and can be promoted to a standalone read-write server in another region, which fits a recovery in minutes with a small data-loss window. Geo-restore from geo-redundant backups also works after a regional loss, but it rebuilds the server from backups, which takes far longer, and the data can be up to an hour old. Zone-redundant high availability keeps its standby in the same region, so a regional outage takes it down too, and a longer retention period only extends how far back a restore can reach, not where the copies are held.

q: A TCP-based game backend runs behind Standard public load balancers in East US and West Europe. Players need one static IP address, automatic routing to the closest healthy region, and fast failover, with client IP addresses preserved. Which service should you add?
opts: Azure Application Gateway v2 deployed in each of the two regions
Azure Traffic Manager using the performance routing method
Azure Front Door Standard with both load balancers as origins
Global tier Azure Load Balancer above the regional ones
why: The global load balancer provides a single static anycast IP address, geo-proximity routing to the closest healthy regional load balancer, and preserves client IPs for TCP and UDP traffic. Traffic Manager works at the DNS level and is subject to caching, Front Door and Application Gateway handle HTTP and HTTPS rather than arbitrary TCP.

q: Three VMs run a stateless web tier in one datacenter, in a single availability set. The company needs the 99.99 percent VM SLA. What is the minimum change that achieves it?
opts: Move the VMs to a larger size family with accelerated networking enabled on each NIC
Place all three VMs in a proximity placement group within the same datacenter
Deploy two or more VMs across zones behind a zone-redundant load balancer
Add two more VMs to the availability set and switch all of them to Premium SSD disks
why: The 99.99 percent SLA requires two or more VMs deployed across availability zones, and a zone-redundant entry point avoids a single zonal dependency. An availability set offers 99.95 percent regardless of size or disks, and neither VM size nor proximity placement affects the SLA tier.

q: A security architect wants one portal view that shows which VMs, databases, and file shares across 25 subscriptions are protected by backup or disaster recovery and which are not. Which should you use?
opts: Azure Advisor cost recommendations
Log Analytics workbook for virtual machine inventory only
A Recovery Services vault in each subscription
Resiliency in Azure
why: Resiliency in Azure, the new name of the Business Continuity Center, shows protected and unprotected resources across subscriptions and solutions in one place. Advisor cost recommendations do not measure protection, an inventory workbook does not know protection status, and individual vaults only see their own items.

q: Which two statements about Azure SQL Database backups are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Long-term retention can keep full backups for up to 10 years
Backups must be configured with a Recovery Services vault policy
Long-term retention keeps log backups so that any second can be restored for years
Point-in-time restore retention defaults to 7 days and can be set from 1 to 35 days
why: Automated backups are on by default with a 7-day point-in-time retention that can be changed from 1 to 35 days, and long-term retention can keep full backups for up to 10 years. Long-term retention keeps full backups, not log backups, so it cannot restore to any second, and Azure SQL Database does not use a vault policy for these built-in backups.

q: Operational backup for Azure Blob Storage protects data from the deletion of the storage account because the backup data is stored in a Backup vault.
opts: True
False
why: Operational backup is a continuous, local solution whose data stays inside the source storage account and is not transferred to the Backup vault. Vaulted backup copies data to a vault and protects against the loss of the account.

q: A global tier Azure Load Balancer can distribute TCP and UDP traffic to the closest healthy regional load balancer and preserves the client IP address.
opts: True
False
why: The global tier uses a static anycast IP address, geo-proximity routing, and client IP preservation in front of regional Standard load balancers, and works for TCP and UDP traffic.

q: A team will run microservices as containers. They must scale on HTTP load and on queue length, including down to zero instances when idle, and they do not want to operate Kubernetes node pools or cluster upgrades. Which compute service fits?
opts: Azure Container Instances container groups
Azure Kubernetes Service with the KEDA add-on
Azure Container Apps
Azure App Service with containers and autoscale rules
why: Container Apps provides built-in HTTP and event-driven scaling, including scale to zero, with no cluster to manage. AKS with KEDA can scale the same way, but the team would still own node pools, upgrades, and cluster configuration. An App Service plan keeps at least one instance running, so it cannot scale to zero. Container Instances runs container groups with no autoscaler of its own.

q: A queue-triggered job runs briefly a few times a day. The company wants no compute charge while the job is idle and no servers to manage. Which hosting option fits?
opts: An App Service plan with Always On enabled
Azure Container Apps with a minimum of one replica
Azure Functions on a Premium plan with one pre-warmed instance
Azure Functions on a Consumption plan
why: A Consumption plan bills per execution and scales to zero, so an idle job costs nothing. A Premium plan keeps at least one pre-warmed instance running and bills for it continuously. A Container Apps app with a minimum of one replica also pays for that replica while idle. An App Service plan is billed for its reserved instances whether or not any code runs.

q: A dozen application teams each own a VNet in one region. All must reach a shared firewall, VPN gateway, and DNS service, but must not reach each other's VNets, and the team wants that isolation without adding custom routing. Which topology fits?
opts: Full-mesh peering between all application VNets and the hub
Hub-and-spoke, with each application VNet peered only to the hub VNet
Virtual WAN, with every VNet connected to the hub's default route table
One shared VNet with a subnet and network security group per team
why: Peering is non-transitive, so spokes peered only to the hub reach the shared services but cannot reach one another by default; no routing work is needed for isolation. In Virtual WAN, VNets connected to a hub's default route table can reach each other, so isolation would need custom route tables. Full-mesh peering creates direct spoke-to-spoke paths. A single shared VNet abandons the separate VNets each team owns and relies on NSG rules for isolation.

q: A trading firm needs private, predictable-latency connectivity from its datacenter to Azure. The connection must survive an ExpressRoute path failure, the firm wants the lowest added cost, and a few minutes of higher latency during a failure are acceptable. What should you recommend?
opts: A second ExpressRoute circuit at a different peering location
ExpressRoute Global Reach linking the datacenter to a second on-premises site
An active-active VPN gateway with two Site-to-Site tunnels over separate internet links
ExpressRoute as the primary path, with a Site-to-Site VPN configured as the failover path
why: ExpressRoute provides the predictable private path, and a Site-to-Site VPN can coexist with it as a lower-cost backup that takes over if the circuit fails; the extra latency during a failover is acceptable here. A second circuit at another peering location is the most resilient design but adds the cost of a whole circuit, which the firm wants to avoid. Two VPN tunnels are resilient but give up the predictability of a private circuit entirely. Global Reach links on-premises sites to each other through the Microsoft backbone and does not add a backup path into Azure.

q: A global retailer needs one entry point that sends users to the nearest healthy regional deployment, fails over in seconds rather than waiting on DNS caches, caches static content at the edge, and applies a single WAF policy to all regions. Which should you use?
opts: Azure CDN in front of a Standard Load Balancer in each region
Azure Front Door with a global WAF policy
Azure Traffic Manager with an Application Gateway WAF in each region
A single regional Application Gateway v2 with autoscale and WAF
why: Front Door is a global layer-7 entry point: it routes by latency and health at the edge with real data-plane failover, caches content at the edge, and enforces one WAF policy centrally. Traffic Manager only answers DNS queries, so failover is bounded by DNS TTL and client caching, and the WAF would have to be configured in every region. A single Application Gateway is regional. A CDN caches content but has no application-aware routing or WAF of its own, and a Standard Load Balancer works at layer 4 within one region.

q: A hub-and-spoke network must limit workloads' outbound internet traffic to a list of approved domain names, some with wildcards, and log every allowed and denied connection centrally, without maintaining rules on each subnet. Which resource should you deploy in the hub?
opts: A NAT gateway on each spoke subnet
Azure Firewall with application rules in a firewall policy
An Application Gateway with WAF in the hub
Network security groups on each spoke subnet that use service tags
why: Azure Firewall application rules filter outbound traffic by FQDN, including wildcards, and its logs are centralized, all managed once in the hub. NSGs filter on IP address, port, and protocol, and service tags only name Microsoft-managed address ranges, so they cannot express arbitrary approved domains and would have to be maintained on every subnet. A NAT gateway provides outbound addresses and does no filtering. An Application Gateway with WAF protects inbound web traffic to your apps, not outbound traffic from workloads.

q: Before migrating 400 on-premises VMs, a team must discover them, map which servers communicate with each other so they can be moved in dependent groups, and get right-sized Azure VM recommendations from actual utilization. Which should anchor this phase?
opts: Azure Migrate: Server Migration, replicating the VMs to Azure
Azure Migrate discovery and assessment with dependency analysis
Azure Advisor recommendations for the subscription the VMs will land in
The Azure TCO Calculator, using server counts and sizes entered by hand
why: Azure Migrate's discovery and assessment collects configuration and performance data from the on-premises VMs, recommends right-sized Azure VMs and costs, and its dependency analysis shows server-to-server connections so related servers move together. The TCO Calculator works from numbers someone types in, so it discovers nothing and cannot see utilization or dependencies. Server Migration is the replication and cutover tool used after assessment. Advisor analyzes resources that are already running in Azure.

q: An order system must process each customer's orders strictly in the sequence submitted, discard duplicate submissions, and set poison messages aside for review. Which service should it use?
opts: Azure Event Hubs with the customer ID as the partition key
Azure Event Grid with an event subscription per customer
An Azure Service Bus queue with sessions enabled
Azure Storage queues with a visibility timeout
why: Service Bus sessions give first-in-first-out processing per customer, duplicate detection discards repeats, and the dead-letter queue sets poison messages aside. Storage queues offer no FIFO guarantee or built-in duplicate detection. Event Hubs keeps order within a partition, but it is a streaming ingestion service with no dead-lettering or duplicate detection. Event Grid pushes discrete event notifications and does not provide ordered queue processing.

q: A company exposes backend APIs hosted on VMs, App Service, and AKS to external partners. Each partner needs its own subscription key and rate limit, and some responses must be transformed from XML to JSON. Which service should sit in front of the backends?
opts: Azure Front Door with a rules engine
Azure Logic Apps with an HTTP trigger
Azure Application Gateway with path-based routing rules
Azure API Management with products and policies
why: API Management fronts any backend with per-consumer subscriptions and keys, rate limits and quotas, and policies that transform requests and responses, plus versioning and a developer portal. Application Gateway and Front Door can route by path to different backends, but they do not issue per-partner keys, enforce per-consumer quotas, or transform payloads as an API product. Logic Apps can be made to behave like an API, but it is a workflow engine, not an API gateway.

q: An integration team must connect a SaaS CRM, an on-premises ERP through a data gateway, and SharePoint. Designers want a visual designer with prebuilt connectors, and the flows must be deployed from source control through Bicep pipelines, run under Azure RBAC, and be monitored in Azure Monitor. Which service fits?
opts: Azure Functions with Durable Functions
Power Automate cloud flows
Azure Data Factory pipelines
Azure Logic Apps
why: Logic Apps provides a visual designer and hundreds of prebuilt connectors as an Azure resource, so workflows deploy with Bicep or ARM, are governed by Azure RBAC, and emit telemetry to Azure Monitor. Power Automate targets business users inside the Power Platform, with a different governance and deployment model. Functions with Durable Functions can orchestrate the same logic but are code-first, with no designer or prebuilt connector catalog. Data Factory moves and transforms data on schedules rather than orchestrating event-driven business workflows.

q: When a Traffic Manager endpoint fails its health probes, clients are redirected to a healthy endpoint immediately, regardless of DNS caching.
opts: True
False
why: Traffic Manager only changes the DNS answers it returns. Clients and resolvers that cached the old answer keep using it until the record's TTL expires, so failover is delayed by the probing interval plus the TTL. Front Door sits in the data path and can fail over without waiting on DNS caches.

q: A Virtual WAN hub inspects and filters traffic between connected VNets on its own, so Azure Firewall is not needed to enforce filtering rules between them.
opts: True
False
why: A virtual hub is a managed routing and connectivity construct; it does not filter traffic by itself. To inspect and filter traffic through the hub, Azure Firewall or a supported third-party security solution is deployed into it, making it a secured virtual hub, and routing configuration steers traffic through that firewall.

q: Which two statements correctly distinguish Azure Front Door from Azure Application Gateway? (Choose two.)
opts: Application Gateway can route users to the nearest of several regions with no service in front of it
Application Gateway lives in a dedicated subnet of your VNet; Front Door is a global service outside any VNet
Front Door can terminate TLS at the edge but cannot route requests by URL path
Application Gateway includes edge caching through built-in integration with Azure CDN
Front Door can use origins outside Azure, such as an on-premises or other-cloud endpoint with a public address
why: Application Gateway is deployed into a subnet of a customer VNet and serves one region, while Front Door is a global edge service that can front any origin reachable by a public address, inside or outside Azure. Application Gateway cannot steer users between regions by itself, which is why Front Door or Traffic Manager sits in front of regional gateways. Front Door does route by URL path, and edge caching is a Front Door capability, not an Application Gateway one.

q: Which two statements describe workloads that would justify choosing AKS over Azure Container Apps? (Choose two.)
opts: The team wants to scale to zero on HTTP traffic and queue length
The team wants to avoid cluster upgrades and node pool management
The workload needs DaemonSets and full control over node pool configuration
The team writes custom Kubernetes operators and needs direct access to the Kubernetes API
The team wants per-request billing with no infrastructure to size
why: Direct Kubernetes API access for custom operators, and DaemonSets or node-pool-level control, are things Container Apps deliberately hides, so they point to AKS. Scale to zero on HTTP or queue triggers, avoiding cluster upgrades and node pools, and consumption-style billing are precisely the reasons to prefer Container Apps.

q: Which two statements about Azure ExpressRoute are true? (Choose two.)
opts: ExpressRoute encrypts traffic end to end by default, so VPN encryption is unnecessary
Microsoft peering is the routing domain used to reach VNet private IP addresses
Traffic on an ExpressRoute circuit is private but not encrypted by default
An ExpressRoute gateway and a VPN gateway must be placed in separate virtual networks
Private peering is the routing domain used to reach VNet resources by their private IP addresses
why: A circuit keeps traffic off the public internet, but private is not the same as encrypted: encryption requires something like IPsec over the circuit or MACsec on ExpressRoute Direct. Private peering is the domain that reaches VNet private addresses, whereas Microsoft peering is used for Microsoft online services and the public endpoints of Azure PaaS services. ExpressRoute and VPN gateways can coexist in one VNet, which is how a VPN is configured as a backup.

q: An on-premises application connects to Azure over ExpressRoute and must reach an Azure SQL Database privately, with no traffic crossing the public internet, and the server's public endpoint must be disabled. Which networking feature enables this?
opts: ExpressRoute Microsoft peering with a route filter that includes Azure SQL
A private endpoint for the SQL server, in a VNet connected to the ExpressRoute circuit
A firewall rule on the SQL server allowing the on-premises public IP range
A service endpoint on the subnet that hosts the ExpressRoute gateway
why: A private endpoint gives the SQL server a private IP address in a VNet; on-premises clients reach that address through the circuit's private peering, and the public endpoint can be disabled. A service endpoint only helps traffic that originates in the subnet and still targets the public endpoint. Microsoft peering carries traffic to the service's public endpoint, which this design wants disabled. A firewall rule allowing public addresses still depends on the public endpoint.

q: Backend VMs span all three availability zones, and the application uses a non-HTTP TCP protocol. The load balancer's frontend IP address must stay available if an entire zone fails, with one frontend address for clients. Which configuration meets this?
opts: A Basic Load Balancer (a retired SKU) with VMs from all three zones in its backend pool
Three Standard Load Balancers, one per zone, behind Traffic Manager
A Standard Load Balancer with a zonal frontend pinned to zone 1
A Standard Load Balancer with a zone-redundant frontend IP configuration
why: A zone-redundant frontend IP is served from all zones at once, so a single address keeps working when a zone fails. A zonal frontend lives in one zone, so losing that zone takes the address down even though backends in other zones are healthy. The Basic SKU (now retired) has no zone support. Three load balancers behind Traffic Manager give three addresses and DNS-based failover, which is more complex and slower than the single zone-redundant address the requirement describes.

q: Two spoke VNets that are each peered only to a hub can exchange traffic if the hub hosts an Azure Firewall and user-defined routes send spoke traffic to it.
opts: True
False
why: Peering itself is non-transitive, but a firewall or network virtual appliance in the hub can forward traffic between spokes when route tables send it there. This is the standard way to allow controlled, inspected spoke-to-spoke traffic in a hub-and-spoke design, rather than peering the spokes directly.

q: Which two statements about Azure Bastion are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Bastion must be deployed into a dedicated subnet named AzureBastionSubnet
Each spoke VNet needs its own Bastion host because Bastion cannot work across VNet peering
The target VM needs a public IP address and an NSG rule allowing RDP or SSH from the internet
A Bastion host deployed in a hub VNet can reach VMs in peered spoke VNets
An agent must be installed on each target VM before Bastion can connect
why: Bastion works across VNet peering, so one host in the hub serves peered spokes, and it requires a subnet named AzureBastionSubnet. Targets need no public IP, because Bastion connects to their private addresses, and no agent, since the session is brokered through the portal over TLS.

q: A workload behind Azure Front Door serves cached static assets and dynamic API calls that must keep reaching the same regional backend for a given user session. How should you configure Front Door so the API calls stay pinned without breaking static caching?
opts: Place Traffic Manager with priority routing in front of Front Door to hold each user on one region
Send API paths to an origin group with session affinity on, and static paths to a cached route
Disable caching on every route so each request is evaluated for routing again
Raise the origin group's latency sensitivity so the same origin usually wins each request
why: Session affinity is set on the origin group and caching is set per route, so splitting the paths gives each kind of request the behavior it needs. Disabling caching everywhere gives up a working optimization and does not pin sessions anyway. Putting Traffic Manager in front adds a DNS layer that cannot pin a session to one backend behind Front Door. Latency sensitivity only widens which origins count as fastest; it does not guarantee the same origin each time.

q: Azure Bastion is deployed in a hub VNet. Spoke VMs have only private IPs, and each spoke subnet has an NSG that denies other inbound traffic. Administrators cannot connect through Bastion. What should you change?
opts: Remove the NSGs from the spoke subnets, because Bastion connections bypass NSG evaluation
Assign a public IP to each VM and restrict it to Bastion's public IP in the NSG
Add an inbound rule to the spoke NSGs allowing RDP and SSH from the AzureBastionSubnet address range
Allow RDP and SSH from the Internet service tag, because Bastion connects from public addresses
why: Bastion reaches the VM's private IP from the AzureBastionSubnet, and the VM's NSG still evaluates that traffic, so it needs an inbound allow rule scoped to that subnet's address range. NSGs are not bypassed, and removing them would drop a layer of defense. Bastion's connection to the VM originates from its subnet's private addresses, not the internet, so allowing the Internet tag is both unnecessary and too broad. Giving each VM a public IP defeats the purpose of using Bastion.

q: Security requires examining the contents of outbound HTTPS traffic from the spokes for malicious payloads and detecting known attack signatures, with the capability managed centrally in the hub. Which should you deploy?
opts: Azure Firewall Premium with TLS decryption and IDPS
Azure Firewall Standard with threat intelligence filtering
Network security group flow logs with Traffic Analytics
Azure Firewall Basic with application rules
why: Only the Premium SKU can decrypt outbound TLS so the contents can be examined, and it adds a signature-based intrusion detection and prevention system (IDPS), both managed centrally in the hub. Standard filters on FQDNs, network rules, and threat intelligence but cannot look inside encrypted payloads. NSG flow logs (being retired on 30 September 2027 in favor of virtual network flow logs) record who talked to whom and do not inspect content. The Basic SKU is a reduced-feature option intended for small environments.

q: A storage account has a private endpoint, and VNet clients resolve its name to the private IP through a linked Private DNS zone. On-premises clients connected over ExpressRoute still resolve the name to the public IP. What should you add?
opts: An A record for the storage account name in a public Azure DNS zone, pointing to the private IP
A conditional forwarder on the on-premises DNS servers that targets a DNS resolver in the VNet
A service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on the gateway subnet so on-premises traffic stays private
A conditional forwarder on the on-premises DNS servers pointing to the address 168.63.129.16
why: Private DNS zone records can only be resolved from linked VNets, so on-premises DNS must forward the relevant queries to something in Azure that can answer them, such as an Azure DNS Private Resolver inbound endpoint or a DNS forwarder VM in the VNet. The address 168.63.129.16 is a virtual IP reachable only from inside Azure, so on-premises servers cannot use it. A public DNS zone would publish a private address on the internet, and the storage service's own public domain is not a zone the customer controls. A service endpoint gives on-premises traffic no private path and does nothing for name resolution.

q: A subnet full of backend VMs behind a Standard Load Balancer is making a very high volume of outbound connections to a handful of external API endpoints, and administrators see intermittent failures consistent with SNAT port exhaustion. Which change most directly addresses this?
opts: Associate a NAT gateway with the subnet to provide dedicated outbound SNAT capacity
Add an inbound NAT rule to the load balancer for each VM
Enable zone redundancy on the load balancer's frontend IP configuration
Lower the idle timeout and enable TCP reset on the load-balancing rules
why: A NAT gateway provides a much larger, dedicated pool of outbound SNAT ports for a subnet, directly relieving the exhaustion a Standard Load Balancer's default outbound behavior can hit under heavy connection volume. Lowering the idle timeout and enabling TCP reset releases ports sooner, which can ease the symptom but adds no capacity. Inbound NAT rules affect inbound traffic to specific VMs, not outbound SNAT. Zone redundancy on the frontend addresses availability across zones, not port exhaustion.

q: An Ultra Disk can be used as the operating system disk of a virtual machine.
opts: True
False
why: Ultra disks are data disks only; an OS disk uses a Standard SSD, Premium SSD, or Standard HDD managed disk. Ultra Disk is chosen for latency-sensitive data volumes where IOPS and throughput must be tuned independently of capacity.

q: Which two statements about Virtual Machine Scale Sets are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Autoscale rules can be based on CPU percentage but not on a schedule or on queue length
Autoscale changes how many instances run; it does not resize the VM SKU of existing instances
Spreading a scale set across zones keeps the tier running if the whole region is lost
Autoscale can move instances from Standard SSD to Premium SSD disks when load rises
Instances of one scale set can be spread across multiple availability zones
why: Autoscale adds or removes instances, so it is scale out and in, not a change of VM size, and instances can be distributed across zones for zone-level resilience. Zones sit inside one region, so they do not survive a regional outage, autoscale does not change disk types, and rules can be driven by metrics such as queue length as well as by a schedule.

q: An organization wants to apply the same Azure Policy assignments, RBAC roles, and Azure Monitor collection it uses for its Azure VMs to servers that will stay in its own datacenter indefinitely, on hardware it already owns. Which service should it use?
opts: Azure Local clusters in the datacenter
Azure Arc-enabled servers
Azure Migrate with an on-premises appliance
Azure Lighthouse delegated resource management
why: Arc-enabled servers project non-Azure machines as Azure resources, so Policy, RBAC, and Monitor apply without moving the workload or replacing the hardware. Azure Local (formerly Azure Stack HCI) is a hosting platform that runs on validated hardware, not a management layer for existing servers. Azure Migrate prepares workloads to move to Azure, which is not the plan. Lighthouse delegates management across Azure tenants and does not extend Azure management to machines outside Azure.

q: A software company wants enterprise customers to reach its multi-tenant SaaS service privately from their own VNets, without traffic crossing the public internet. Customers' address spaces overlap with each other and with the company's. What should the company configure behind its service?
opts: A public IP address with NSG rules scoped to each customer's range
Azure Private Link service, reached through customers' own private endpoints
A service endpoint on the subnet that hosts the company's service
VNet peering between the company's VNet and every customer's VNet
why: Private Link service publishes the service behind a Standard Load Balancer, and each customer connects through a private endpoint whose address comes from the customer's own VNet; traffic is translated on the provider side, so overlapping address spaces do not matter. VNet peering cannot connect networks with overlapping address ranges and does not scale to many customers. A service endpoint only secures traffic from the company's own subnet to Azure PaaS services. A public IP with NSG rules still relies on a public endpoint.

q: To expose an API Management instance to external partners, the instance must be deployed in external VNet mode, because an internal-mode instance cannot be reached from the internet.
opts: True
False
why: An internal-mode instance has only private endpoints, but it can still be published externally by placing an Application Gateway with a public frontend in front of it. That is a common pattern: the public entry point provides WAF and TLS handling while the API Management gateway itself stays private.

q: Backend VMs behind a Basic load balancer (a SKU since retired) served public HTTP traffic with no NSG attached anywhere. After the team upgrades to a Standard load balancer and Standard public IP, clients can no longer reach the VMs, though the load-balancing rules are unchanged. What should you do?
opts: Enable HA ports on the load-balancing rule to accept traffic on every port
Add the VMs' NICs to an application security group that names the web tier
Associate an NSG that allows inbound traffic on the application port
Add an outbound rule to the load balancer so return traffic is permitted
why: The Standard SKU is closed to inbound traffic until an NSG explicitly allows it, whereas Basic accepted inbound traffic with no NSG at all, so associating an NSG with an allow rule for the application port restores access. An application security group is only a way to name groups of NICs inside NSG rules; without an NSG allow rule it permits nothing. Outbound rules govern SNAT for outbound connections, not inbound reachability. HA ports applies to internal load balancers and does not open anything.

q: Which two statements about Azure Arc are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Arc-enabled servers must be migrated to Azure VMs before Azure Policy can be applied to them
Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters running outside Azure can be configured from Azure with GitOps
Arc requires a site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute connection for its agent to reach Azure
Azure Policy guest configuration can assess the settings inside Arc-enabled servers
Arc can manage Windows Server machines but not Linux servers
why: Arc extends Azure management to resources outside Azure: Kubernetes clusters can be configured declaratively with GitOps, and Policy guest configuration audits settings inside the OS of Arc-enabled servers. The Connected Machine agent needs only outbound HTTPS connectivity, optionally through Private Link, not a VPN or ExpressRoute link. Servers stay where they are, and Linux servers are supported alongside Windows Server.

q: A studio must render 40,000 independent frames every night within a few hours. The work is interruptible and each frame can be retried, and the team wants Azure to schedule tasks and scale the compute automatically at the lowest cost. What should you recommend?
opts: An AKS cluster with a fixed set of on-demand nodes
Azure Batch with a pool of Spot VMs
A single large VM with a scheduled task
Azure Functions on the Consumption plan
why: Batch manages pools, schedules tasks across nodes, scales automatically, and supports Spot VMs for interruptible work, which also lowers cost. One VM is neither scalable nor resilient, a fixed set of on-demand nodes wastes money and still needs a scheduler, and Functions has execution time and sizing limits that do not suit heavy rendering.

q: A software vendor licenses a database engine per physical core and must guarantee that its VMs run only on servers dedicated to the company for compliance reasons. Which Azure compute option should you recommend?
opts: Proximity placement groups
An availability set with five fault domains
Azure Spot Virtual Machines
Azure Dedicated Host
why: Dedicated Host provides single-tenant physical servers, which supports per-core licensing and isolation requirements. Spot VMs run on spare capacity and can be evicted, proximity placement groups influence latency, and an availability set spreads VMs across racks without making them single-tenant.

q: A healthcare company must run an application whose data stays encrypted in memory while being processed, so that even the cloud operator cannot read it. The application can run in a VM without code changes. Which solution should you recommend?
opts: Azure Disk Encryption with BitLocker
Confidential VMs
Storage account infrastructure encryption
A VM with an Azure Hybrid Benefit license
why: Confidential VMs run in a hardware-based trusted execution environment that protects data in use, with no application changes. Disk encryption and storage encryption protect data at rest, and a licensing benefit has nothing to do with data protection.

q: A company must leave its datacenter in 10 weeks. It runs 800 VMware VMs with in-house tooling for vSphere, and the apps cannot be re-IP'd or re-platformed. Which target minimizes change and time?
opts: Azure VMware Solution
Azure App Service Environment
Azure Virtual Machines after converting each disk to VHD
Azure Kubernetes Service with containers built for each app
why: Azure VMware Solution runs the VMware stack on Azure bare metal, so VMs move with the same tools and without conversion or re-IP, which fits the deadline. Converting to native VMs, containerizing, or re-hosting as web apps all require change that the timeline and constraints rule out.

q: A bank's internal web application must run in a dedicated, single-tenant App Service environment injected into its virtual network, reachable only privately, and scale to many instances. What should you use?
opts: App Service Premium v3 plan with regional virtual network integration
Azure Container Instances in the virtual network
App Service Environment with Isolated v2 plans
Static Web Apps with a private endpoint
why: An App Service Environment is deployed into your virtual network on dedicated infrastructure with the Isolated v2 tiers, giving the isolation and scale required. VNet integration only affects outbound calls from a multitenant plan, Container Instances is not App Service, and Static Web Apps hosts static front ends.

q: A workflow integrating 30 SaaS systems must run inside a virtual network, have several workflows grouped in one app, and be developed locally by the integration team. Which hosting option should you recommend?
opts: Logic Apps Standard
Logic Apps Consumption
Azure Data Factory with mapping data flows
Azure Functions Consumption plan
why: Logic Apps Standard is single-tenant, supports virtual network integration, multiple workflows per app, and local development. Consumption is multitenant and pay per execution without those capabilities. A Consumption-plan function would need custom code for SaaS connectors, and Data Factory is a data integration service.

q: After each promotion, an order API receives bursts of about 20,000 requests per minute for roughly two minutes, while the order processor handles about 2,000 per minute and takes several minutes to scale out. No order may be lost, and the processor must not be overloaded. Which design should you use?
opts: The API writes each order to a Service Bus queue, and the processor reads from it at its own pace
The API calls the processor directly and retries with exponential backoff whenever it responds with an error
Autoscale rules that add processor instances when its CPU rises during a burst
A Front Door rate-limit rule that rejects requests above 2,000 per minute
why: A queue between the API and the processor levels the load: the API accepts the whole burst, and the orders wait durably in the queue while the processor works through them at its steady rate, so nothing is lost and the processor is never overloaded. Direct calls with retries keep hitting a processor that is already saturated and push the waiting onto callers, who can give up and lose orders. Autoscale rules react only after the burst has started, and the processor needs minutes to add capacity, so a burst this short is over before it helps. A rate limit protects the processor by rejecting the excess requests, which loses orders. This is the Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern.

q: Existing applications publish telemetry with Apache Kafka producers. The team wants to move to a managed Azure service with minimal code changes, and the data must also be archived automatically to Data Lake Storage. Which service should you choose?
opts: Azure Service Bus Premium with topics
Azure Event Hubs with its Kafka endpoint and Capture
Azure Queue Storage with a function reading the queue
Azure Event Grid with MQTT topics
why: Event Hubs exposes a Kafka-compatible endpoint so producers need little change, and Capture writes events to Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage automatically. Service Bus and Queue Storage are message brokers with different semantics, and Event Grid MQTT targets device messaging and discrete events rather than Kafka streams.

q: An application sometimes calls a downstream service that is failing for minutes at a time. During those periods, the application's threads pile up waiting on timeouts and bring down unrelated features. Which design pattern should you apply to stop calls to the failing dependency?
opts: Claim Check
Cache-Aside
Strangler Fig
Circuit Breaker
why: A circuit breaker stops calls to a dependency that is failing and fails fast until it recovers, which protects other features. Cache-Aside improves read performance, Claim Check handles oversized messages, and Strangler Fig migrates a legacy system gradually.

q: A web application reads product data from Azure SQL Database. Read load is high and the data changes rarely. You want to reduce database load and latency, accepting that entries must be rebuilt from the database if the cache is cleared. Which design should you recommend?
opts: A second Azure SQL Database used as the system of record for reads
Azure Queue Storage in front of every read
Azure Managed Redis used with the cache-aside pattern
Azure Table Storage as the primary store for the products
why: A cache using the cache-aside pattern holds frequently read data in memory and loads it from the database on a miss, which cuts latency and load. A second database adds cost and replication to manage, Table Storage as primary changes the data model, and a queue does not serve reads.

q: A new design uses a caching tier. A colleague proposes Azure Cache for Redis Basic tier. Which is the best advice?
opts: Use Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise, because that tier is supported for many more years
Use Azure Table Storage, because the Redis service has been retired for all tiers
Use the Basic tier, because it adds replication and zone redundancy at no extra cost
Use Azure Managed Redis, since the Basic tier retires on September 30, 2028
why: Azure Managed Redis is the current offering for new designs, and the Basic, Standard, and Premium tiers of Azure Cache for Redis retire on September 30, 2028, while the Enterprise tiers retire on March 31, 2027. The Basic tier has no replication or zone redundancy, and Redis itself is available through Azure Managed Redis.

q: A GitHub Actions workflow deploys Bicep files to Azure. Security forbids long-lived client secrets stored in the repository. What should you configure?
opts: A personal access token of the lead developer stored in the pipeline
A federated credential on a managed identity or app registration using OpenID Connect
A storage account key stored as an encrypted repository secret
A service principal secret stored in the repository and rotated every year
why: Workload identity federation lets the workflow obtain tokens through OpenID Connect without stored secrets. A rotated service principal secret is still a stored secret, and account keys and personal tokens are broad, long-lived credentials tied to people or accounts.

q: A company wants developers to self-serve complete test environments from templates, and proposes building the design on Azure Deployment Environments. What should you tell them?
opts: It needs a Premium Azure DevOps license for each of the developers
It is available only in Azure Government and sovereign cloud regions
It is the recommended successor to Bicep for all new self-service environment designs
The service retires on 22 February 2027, so plan another approach
why: Microsoft has announced that Azure Deployment Environments retires on 22 February 2027 and asks customers to transition to another Microsoft service, Azure service, or partner solution, so a new design should not depend on it. It is not a successor to Bicep and is not limited to Azure Government.

q: A company has assessed 600 VMware VMs and decided to rehost them on Azure VMs. It wants to replicate the VMs while they keep running, run a test migration without affecting production, and cut over each group with a short outage, without installing agents on the guests. What should it use?
opts: Azure Arc-enabled servers
Azure Migrate discovery and assessment with the appliance
Azure Migrate: Server Migration with agentless replication
Azure Data Box with exported VM disk images
why: Server Migration replicates running VMware VMs to Azure through the Azure Migrate appliance without agents on the guests, supports a test migration, and cuts over after a final delta sync, so the outage is short. Discovery and assessment sizes and prices the move but replicates nothing, and Arc-enabled servers projects machines into Azure for management without moving them. Shipping exported disk images offline gives no continuous replication and a long outage at cutover.

q: A company is moving a SQL Server instance that uses SQL Agent jobs and cross-database queries to a managed platform, and wants minimal downtime while the on-premises instance keeps running until cutover. Which migration path should you recommend?
opts: Managed Instance with the Managed Instance link for replication
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, loaded with Data Factory pipelines
A single Azure SQL database, using a BACPAC export during a weekend window
SQL Server on a VM, using a nightly file copy of the data files
why: Managed Instance supports SQL Agent and cross-database queries, and the link replicates in near real time so cutover is short. A single database does not support those features, a BACPAC means long downtime, and file copies and a NoSQL conversion do not meet the compatibility or downtime goals.

q: A film archive must move 300 TB of files from a remote site with a 20 Mbps connection to Azure Storage as a one-time migration. Which option should you recommend?
opts: Azure File Sync with a single server endpoint
AzCopy over the existing 20 Mbps connection
Azure Data Box appliances shipped to the site
Azure Storage Mover over the existing connection
why: At 20 Mbps, 300 TB would take years to upload, so an offline appliance is appropriate, as Data Box suits data over about 40 TB with little network capacity. AzCopy and Storage Mover are online tools limited by the link, and File Sync keeps a file server in step over the network.

q: An organization copies 8 TB of file shares from on-premises NAS devices and from an AWS S3 bucket to Azure Storage, with repeatable jobs and minimal downtime for the workloads, over a fast connection. Which service is built for this?
opts: Azure Data Box Disk
Azure Storage Mover
Azure Site Recovery
Azure Import/Export with hard drives
why: Storage Mover is a managed service for migrating files and folders from on-premises or AWS S3 to Azure Storage with minimal downtime and repeatable jobs. Data Box and drive shipping are offline methods that are not needed with a fast connection, and Site Recovery replicates VMs.

q: A company protects 150 public IP addresses across several virtual networks. It wants DDoS rapid response support, cost protection for scale-out charges during an attack, and discounts on its Web Application Firewall. Which should you choose?
opts: A network security group on each subnet
DDoS IP Protection on each public IP address
The basic DDoS infrastructure protection that every public IP gets
DDoS Network Protection on the virtual networks
why: Network Protection includes rapid response support, cost protection, and WAF discounts, and covers many IPs in a virtual network, while IP Protection omits those features. Basic infrastructure protection offers no such extras, and an NSG is not a DDoS service.

q: Two network virtual appliances in a hub exchange routes with Azure virtual networks. The team no longer wants to maintain user-defined routes by hand as spokes are added. Which service should you add?
opts: ExpressRoute FastPath
Azure Route Server
Azure Firewall policy
A NAT gateway on the hub subnet
why: Route Server exchanges routes between NVAs and the Azure network using BGP, so routes update dynamically. A firewall policy governs rules rather than routing, a NAT gateway provides outbound translation, and FastPath optimizes ExpressRoute data paths.

q: An organization wants to restrict public network access to several storage accounts, Key Vaults, and SQL servers so that they accept traffic only from approved resources in the same boundary. The resources are not placed in virtual networks. Which feature should you use?
opts: A network security perimeter
A network security group on a subnet
Azure Bastion
A route table with a default route
why: A network security perimeter creates a logical boundary around PaaS resources outside virtual networks and controls their public access with inbound and outbound rules. NSGs and route tables apply to resources in virtual networks, and Bastion is for VM connectivity.

q: A central network team must enforce that no virtual network in the organization allows inbound RDP from the internet, even if an application team creates an NSG rule that allows it. Which feature should you use?
opts: Azure Policy with the Audit effect
Security admin rules in Azure Virtual Network Manager
A user-defined route to a null next hop
A network security group on each application subnet
why: Security admin rules from Virtual Network Manager are evaluated before NSG rules, so a deny cannot be overridden by an application team's NSG. NSGs are owned by application teams, Audit only reports, and a null route breaks all traffic to the prefix rather than blocking one port.

q: Latency-sensitive VMs in one region exchange many small packets and show jitter. The team wants to reduce latency and CPU overhead for networking without changing the application. What should you enable?
opts: A NAT gateway on the subnet that hosts the VMs
Azure Front Door with an origin group that contains the VMs
A network security group with extra allow rules for the traffic
Accelerated networking on the VM network interfaces
why: Accelerated networking bypasses the host virtual switch, giving lower latency, less jitter, and lower CPU use. Front Door and NAT gateway do not affect VM-to-VM traffic inside the region, and more NSG rules do not improve performance.

q: App Service back ends must accept traffic only from Azure Front Door over a private connection, with no public endpoint exposed. Which Front Door tier should you choose?
opts: Azure Front Door Standard with origin IP restrictions
Azure Front Door Premium with Private Link to the origin
Azure Traffic Manager with a Priority profile
Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic)
why: Front Door Premium supports Private Link connections to origins, so the origin can remain private. Standard can only restrict public access by header or IP, Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) retires on September 30, 2027 and is not the recommended basis for a new design, and Traffic Manager is a DNS service with no private connectivity.

q: Which two statements about Azure Batch are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: There is no charge for Batch itself, only for the underlying compute and storage
Batch is a streaming engine for continuous SQL queries over events
Batch runs tasks on pools of compute nodes and can use Spot VMs
Batch requires every task to run on a dedicated physical host
why: Batch schedules tasks across pools of nodes that can include Spot VMs, and you pay for the underlying resources, not for the service. Continuous SQL over streams is Stream Analytics, and tasks do not need dedicated physical hosts.

q: Azure Storage queues are the best choice when messages must be delivered in guaranteed first-in-first-out order with automatic duplicate detection.
opts: True
False
why: Service Bus provides guaranteed FIFO ordering with sessions and automatic duplicate detection. Storage queues are simpler and cheaper but do not provide those guarantees.

q: The Developer tier of Azure API Management is suitable for production workloads because it includes an SLA.
opts: True
False
why: The Developer tier is for non-production use and evaluation, and it does not offer an SLA. Production workloads use Basic, Standard, Premium, or one of the v2 tiers, or Consumption.
